item.title: Philippine Immigration Detention: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-cn907a40-菲律宾移民局拘留所-不交钱-你的遣返程序永远走不通/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-cn907a40-菲律宾移民局拘留所-不交钱-你的遣返程序永远走不通/
item.description: A Chinese surfer held for 41 days in the Philippines saw not a prison but a business with prices posted on everything: a bed, a boxed meal, a phone, a lawyer's fee. Those who don't pay stay for years, sometimes more than a decade.
item.content:encoded:
A Chinese surfer held for 41 days in the Philippines saw not a prison but a business with prices posted on everything: a bed, a boxed meal, a phone, a lawyer's fee. Those who don't pay stay for years, sometimes more than a decade.

StoryFM's Behind Bars series — medium information density but solid detail. The first half is one man's ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers who raise their price on the spot — is where the real value is.

10:05 The Immigration Bureau quoted 1.5 million pesos to walk free on the spot
The night Feili was arrested, an immigration officer pulled him aside and said quietly, "I can help you." After the lawyer communicated with them, the answer came back: give 1.5 million pesos, about 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you can be released immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 or 13 people arrested in the same batch, no one agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing still existed in 2026 and wanted to resolve it through normal legal procedure. But the price of refusing was this: they were transferred from the holding cells of the General Santos police station to the Immigration Bureau detention center in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

18:21 When the phone was taken, the money in Gcash was transferred out
When Feili was detained his phone was confiscated, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed it was normal procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — Gcash being the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days he applied repeatedly and could not get the phone back, until he kept pressing the Chinese consulate and his lawyer, and it was finally returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out — then transferred back the night before he got the phone. There was only about 1,000 RMB in it. Feili says it isn't about the amount; it's that the phone was touched while it wasn't in his hands. His read: many Chinese in Manila working in gray-industry scams go through this same shakedown after arrest, but they don't dare approach the Chinese consulate, because their phones hold a mass of criminal evidence.

24:26 The air conditioning and takeout the Immigration Bureau promised exist — in another form
For those unwilling to buy their own plane ticket for the transfer, the Immigration Bureau works on them in shifts, saying conditions at the Manila bureau are excellent: air conditioning, plenty of freedom, a gym, basketball, takeout delivery, phone use. Feili says they weren't lying — there really is air conditioning, you really can order takeout, it's just another form, a completely different form. They arrived at the main bureau's detention center after 3 a.m. What he saw getting out of the vehicle was a square compound: an outer layer of iron grating, a sheet-metal roof above, iron cages like dog kennels on all sides, and inside them long communal platforms holding several hundred people. At past 3 a.m. many weren't sleeping — bare-chested, in nothing but underwear, they clung to the cage bars to stare at the newcomers. Feili says he and the other foreigners said nothing for several minutes after getting out, then it hit them: the Immigration Bureau had lied to them.

32:38 The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
What Feili heard inside was that this Immigration Bureau detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss in cooperation with the bureau, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities were all newly built by that Chinese boss. Foreigners could just stay, but Chinese who came in had to pay. The cheapest tier, a spot on the communal platform, was 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy pan zong and gambling bosses could pay 50,000 pesos a month, over 6,000 RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — in fact the bed was the same, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a foam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan drawing the cold air into the bed. That is where the Immigration Bureau's earlier promise of "air conditioning inside" came from.

34:38 Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to collect a "rumor fee," saying the facilities were their investment and there was no way to stay for free. Feili said he had no money, that he was here to serve time — how could he be expected to pay as well? The gang boss said in a threatening tone: you're already in here, you don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run through gang divisions, with the Chinese gang monopolizing all food, clothing and daily life for Chinese inmates, operating a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center held about 200 people; when Feili arrived it was the low season and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them from gambling and gray industry. The Chinese gang's staff draw wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, the kitchen helper 5,000 pesos. The pay is very low, but many people can't get out precisely because they have no money for a lawyer, so they can only work to earn.

43:48 A man from Yunnan held over a year; his family thought he died in Southeast Asia
A young man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he had been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken and he was dragged into a compound to run telecom fraud, and when his numbers were poor his supervisor shocked him with a stun baton every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the Immigration Bureau detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own ticket, and you leave — but the Immigration Bureau, in order to extract money, keeps you locked up a long time, and without paying the procedure doesn't move. He had already been held over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he had died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese and translate it into English, and through an introduction from a Japanese man got to see the warden, who had a guard bring Feili's phone so the young man could add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterwards the Immigration Bureau bought a basic phone specifically to solve this problem.

51:29 Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
The only Chinese person Feili talked with at any length came from a scam company. The company's 70 or 80 people had been surrounded by three agencies — the Immigration Bureau together with the police and the NBI. The first shakedown was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet, because there are no cameras in the toilets, and stripping them of everything valuable. The second was the Immigration Bureau negotiating ransoms with the company boss — the quote differed per person, 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos, depending on the negotiator's mood. That company's deal was 3 million pesos per person, over 300,000 RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people, exactly the 30 held on one floor; the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; in his best month he took in 2 million RMB, and bought a house and a car in his small home county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, several hundred thousand was transferred out, and a corrupt cop pinned an illegal gun-possession charge on him, so he couldn't leave.

57:32 A Philippine lawyer raises the price the moment he sees you're Chinese
In Cebu, Feili was introduced by a Lithuanian to a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, over 20,000 RMB, to settle it in four weeks. After Feili reached Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and raised the price on the spot, saying the earlier figure was the old price and the new price required another 120,000 pesos, over 10,000 RMB. Feili decided not to use him and abandoned the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted over 30,000 RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six. Feili says the genuinely reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedural pipeline extremely well, because everyone locked up inside is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for over 30 days, 41 days counting Cebu. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili messaged him.

item.title: Video generation doesn't lack speed anymore — it lacks the director's control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-a16z-视频生成不缺速度了-缺的是导演手里的控制权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-a16z-视频生成不缺速度了-缺的是导演手里的控制权/
item.description: FAL post-trains open-source video models to be an order of magnitude faster and an order of magnitude cheaper than the originals, then concludes: speed is no longer the bottleneck. What's next is controllability over camera, lighting, characters and motion.
item.content:encoded:
FAL post-trains open-source video models to be an order of magnitude faster and an order of magnitude cheaper than the originals, then concludes: speed is no longer the bottleneck. What's next is controllability over camera, lighting, characters and motion.

The first half is hardcore inference-system optimization detail; the second half is Hollywood workflows and a controllability roadmap. High information density, good for forming a judgment.

3:02 Open weights are the precondition for post-training
FAL had run inference for other model labs before, but never had permission to layer capabilities onto the model. Minimax H3 was the first genuinely open-source video model that was also current-generation, could accept reference images, and had an architecture similar to other video models — which is what made FAL decide to go all in on post-training. Gorka says the biggest reason all these optimizations could come together this time is that H3 was the first truly next-generation open-source video model — no weights, no post-training business.

4:02 The whole industry has been compute-constrained since April
Gorka offers a criterion he calls token market fit: whether a person can productively consume a large amount of tokens, on the order of 10K. Demand for video generation is big enough — people in this line of work sit at their computers generating all day and spend thousands of dollars. But since April, the whole industry and FAL itself have been compute-constrained: add however much compute, get however much growth. So FAL keeps hunting for efficiency, releasing the compute it saves to other models, or letting H3 Max generate more tokens.

5:04 System optimization hits a roofline; post-training punches through it
Batuan says the system-level optimization of the past three or four years can at best make the same model 2 to 3 times faster, because the architecture and constraints haven't changed — you're just squeezing the chip harder, and that roofline is real. New post-training plus system-model co-design can go an order of magnitude past that roofline. FAL had practiced on open-source image models before, doing versions of ideogram and flux, and built up post-training infrastructure experience; this time, adding a frontier video model, speed went up by an order of magnitude.

7:10 Raise quality first, then cut steps — the order can't be reversed
Compressing a diffusion model from 50 steps to 20 loses quality, so FAL's approach is to first run post-training and the L pipeline to raise model quality, then layer on the optimization stack, so the final result is equal or better in quality while being an order of magnitude faster. Beyond post-training, there are kernels and systems engineering pushing hardware utilization from the 30-40% typical of inference workloads up to a theoretical 70-80% MFU. And a video model isn't a single call — underneath is a pipeline: first a large LLM expands the prompt, then generation happens in latent space, then decoding back to pixels, plus possibly upscaling depending on the load, and by default none of these components is optimized.

10:19 The Turbo version does a five-second video in 1.5 seconds
A week after H3 Max launched, the team found it could run at 2x speed with quality still in the 97th percentile, so they released H3 Max Turbo: generating a five-second video takes just 1.5 seconds, at half the cost. Gorka's judgment is that these models today are already cheap enough and fast enough — an order of magnitude cheaper than frontier models, more than an order of magnitude faster than frontier — and users don't need faster or cheaper. His bet is that what comes next is raising quality, and controllability — which is exactly the direction of the past two or three weeks.

16:43 Continuous video runs on two minutes of memory, not the last frame
The livestreams Rehan and levels io each made are essentially independent clips: one segment ends, its last frame is fed into the next segment, and the second segment remembers nothing but that last frame. FAL's internal ML team built something else: transitions are more seamless, there are two minutes of memory, when someone walks into the room everyone looks at him, and the scene is continuous. What it remembers is a highly compressed representation of the original video; beyond two minutes, a continuously evolving system prompt maintains overall coherence, so it can remember the last four to eight scenes and stream indefinitely.

29:00 Blender plus a video model equals near-100% controllability
One of the most popular approaches in professional workflows: first render a low-resolution scene with non-AI technology like Blender, then feed that video as a reference to the AI model, and you basically get close to 100% controllability. A week after H3 Max launched, people started generating scenes in Blender with GPT Astra and handing them to H3 Max, because it's fast enough to try many in parallel — opening up an entirely new pipeline. Gorka says the next month or two will be all-in on controllability, so studios and professional creators can get content that fits their use case exactly.

33:03 Hollywood wants small point solutions, not generation from scratch
Gorka says Hollywood is FAL's fastest-growing segment, with usage a year ago at nearly zero. The NARA tool Amazon MGM Studios released runs mainly on FAL's infrastructure. What Hollywood wants isn't to generate everything from scratch, but small point solutions: extend a video a bit, change camera control, change lighting. There's a disconnect between what research labs are building and what creators actually need, and FAL wants to close that gap with post-training projects. The other half of the problem is legal and data residency — Seedance now has US hosting too — and Gorka thinks Hollywood's AI usage will grow 10x, 100x in the coming months.

item.title: Litigation Risk for Financial Advisors: The Retailisation of Private Assets Is Creating a Regulatory Gap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-rationalreminder-理财顾问的诉讼风险-私人资产零售化正在制造监管缺口/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-rationalreminder-理财顾问的诉讼风险-私人资产零售化正在制造监管缺口/
item.description: Private assets, long confined to accredited investors, are now open to the public without the protections that traditionally accompany a public offering — practices normalised in an institutional setting become major litigation risk once ordinary investors are in the room.
item.content:encoded:
Private assets, long confined to accredited investors, are now open to the public without the protections that traditionally accompany a public offering — practices normalised in an institutional setting become major litigation risk once ordinary investors are in the room.

This episode breaks down advisor practice risk from a litigator's perspective, with high information density — especially useful for anyone in wealth management, private asset sales or compliance.

1:02 Winning a case turns on evidence, not on fault
Taylor says a successful negligence claim almost always requires a failure in the suitability analysis first — KYC information not gathered accurately, the product not properly understood. But "there was a failure" is not the same as "it can be proven." He splits the question into "what people know" and "what people can prove," saying the two rarely line up perfectly and that it is the latter that ultimately drives the analysis. On evidence, the strongest thing is an advisor who used the same portfolio for everyone: a pile of people with identical portfolios but completely different life circumstances turns "he said, she said" into "he said, she said, she said, he said, they said" — far more persuasive to a judge than one person's unilateral account.

2:03 The trading record is itself a red flag
Taylor lists a string of behaviours that are almost impossible to explain rationally: concentrations above 80%–90% (he has seen it, and in small caps), churning done purely to generate commissions, and double dipping on multi-account clients — buying in a commission-based account first, then moving the assets into a fee-based or AUM-based account for no reason. Then there are trades entered without any confirmation, and off-book communications. He says these are powerful because in most cases the advisor or the firm simply cannot offer a reasonable explanation.

5:07 Communication that goes from eager to absent is a warning sign
Taylor describes a pattern that is not rare: extremely dense, solicitous communication while winning the account, then one or two contacts a year once the account is won — the bare minimum of communication. He thinks that enormous drop-off is itself a problem. Another signal is that nobody ever talks to you about changed life circumstances — retirement, a layoff, the death of a breadwinner, a new child — all of which should feed into the recommendation. If you look back and think "so much happened and we never discussed whether my needs had changed," that does not necessarily mean something went wrong, but it is worth getting a second set of eyes on it.

7:07 Check the regulatory complaint record before you hire
Taylor says this is one of the strongest pre-hire signals, and it costs almost nothing: if the person is regulated (he says most large dealers are), complaint and investigation records are public information, and checking takes under 5 minutes. The mechanism he describes is that these claims commonly involve someone who had a small complaint first, was watched closely for a while, then reverted to form — only at a much larger scale. He also cautions that past outcomes do not necessarily predict the future, but this is a very worthwhile piece of information to feed into the decision.

8:08 What victims share is vulnerability, not stupidity
Taylor says these investors have a lot in common, and it is almost always some form of vulnerability: advanced age, lower education, language barriers — official forms and statements exist only in the two official languages, English and French, so clients who struggle to understand rely more heavily on the advisor, and people naturally seek out someone they can communicate with, which stacks another layer of asymmetry on top. Another group is people who suddenly come into money: a life insurance payout, a large inheritance, where they are simultaneously dealing with a drastically changed financial situation and a negative life event. He has personally advised a lottery winner and has heard peers describe the same situation.

39:28 Fee structures are the next litigation goldmine
Taylor says fees are the second big indicator after disclosure, and there is already a wave of class actions built around fees; some fee types can no longer be charged because of legislative changes — for example, charging on an advisory basis in a non-advisory account. He expects future litigation to centre on "how fees are calculated," and names private asset managers as particularly fertile ground for lawsuits. For people in wealth management, this means the fee basis baked into product design is itself legal risk exposure, not just a commercial choice.

41:29 Pension funds manage litigation claims as an asset
Taylor cites a Stanford Law Review article from twenty years ago titled Letting Billions Slip Through Your Fingers: at the time, many pension funds and other asset managers simply did not participate in securities class action settlements, effectively leaving money on the table — possibly because they had not kept the records needed to participate, or because the decision-makers were philosophically opposed to suing. US pension funds later broadly retained monitoring counsel, who are not paid, to flag potential claims, and built into their compliance and committee structures a decision process for "whether to participate in litigation, and in what capacity." Taylor says Canada has not caught up here. His key judgment: under a fiduciary standard, a claim in litigation is itself an asset, it can be sold, and it should be managed like any other asset.

47:32 Private assets strip out the people who digest information
Taylor reduces the problem with private assets to two umbrella issues: less information and less regulation, and both are by design. In public markets, the information asymmetry created by the separation of ownership and control is smoothed out by a set of checks: periodic financials, periodic audits, third-party verification, regulators, and a large population of people whose job is to digest and disseminate information — equity analysts track companies, what analysts say gets picked up by journalists, and an ordinary person opening the Globe and Mail can at least get a rough sense of what happened last quarter at a TSX company. Private assets strip all of that away: statutory reporting requirements are extremely limited, there is no comparable analyst coverage, and the raw information that is available is itself far scarcer.

item.title: A justice once blocked a polling place; forty years later it became a national tactic
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-throughline-大法官曾带人堵投票站-四十年后成了全国战术/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-throughline-大法官曾带人堵投票站-四十年后成了全国战术/
item.description: Rehnquist challenged Black voters' eligibility in Phoenix in 1962, and two years later the playbook became a nationwide "Operation Eagle Eye"; meanwhile, Arab workers in Detroit used a wildcat strike to grow political power out of the factories.
item.content:encoded:
Rehnquist challenged Black voters' eligibility in Phoenix in 1962, and two years later the playbook became a nationwide "Operation Eagle Eye"; meanwhile, Arab workers in Detroit used a wildcat strike to grow political power out of the factories.

Two storylines lay out the two paths of the American voting-rights fight: top-down suppression and bottom-up organizing. Medium information density; the Michigan story in the back half is the more valuable part.

0:00 The future chief justice stopped people at the polls
At Rehnquist's 1986 confirmation hearings, the most dramatic part was not his 14 years of judicial record but what he did in Phoenix in the 1960s. Witnesses said he stood outside a polling place, walked up to a Black voter and asked "Are you a qualified voter," demanding the person show documents and read aloud a passage of the Constitution. Rehnquist denied at the hearings that he harassed or intimidated voters, but admitted he had given legal advice to Republicans challenging voters' eligibility at polling places, and sometimes showed up in person. He called it an "election day project"; others called it a "ballot security project." That project later became a national strategy.

8:12 His conservatism took shape in high school
Journalist John A. Jenkins was doing interviews for a Rehnquist biography when his editor told him to dig into "the origins of his conservatism." Rehnquist was born in 1924 in Shorewood, Wisconsin, an all-white community, and went to an all-white high school. He was a senior when Pearl Harbor was attacked; he organized a school assembly called "Wake Up America," joined patriotic groups, and signed up as a block captain to report subversive activity to the FBI. After the war he entered Stanford Law School, finished first in his class, and then clerked for Supreme Court Justice Robert Jackson. Five months later, in 1952, the 28-year-old wrote a memo telling Jackson: you need not vote with the majority in Brown v. Board; there is a more principled position.

13:46 He saw integration as a personal choice, not a federal matter
Rehnquist's position was that integration is a matter of personal choice and should not be imposed on people; it should also be decided by the states, not the federal government. This was a classic conservative stance, and it helped him establish himself among Republican rising stars as an ideological purist. He carried that philosophy with him to Phoenix, which was still dealing with Jim Crow laws and an emerging civil rights movement. When the city council passed an anti-discrimination ordinance, he wrote letters to the editor and spoke at meetings, was noticed, and was encouraged to enter politics. This meant extra scrutiny of voters in Democratic-leaning precincts — Republicans believed many of them were voting illegally.

16:50 The voter-challenge playbook: returned mail means sending people to the polls
Tova Wang, research project director at Harvard Kennedy School's Ash Center, read FBI background-check excerpts: two white Republican challengers, one of them allegedly Rehnquist, at a polling place in an elementary school named for civil rights leader Mary McLeod Bethune on November 6, 1962, facing Black and minority voters, showing them a card with a passage from the Constitution and demanding they read it aloud to prove literacy. The method was: first mail letters into Democratic precincts, and if the mail came back, send challengers to the polls to question eligibility. According to one FBI interview, the plan was to send large numbers of challengers into minority Democratic precincts at peak hours to clog the polling places, intimidate voters or drag things out until they gave up. Arizona law allowed each party to send representatives to challenge suspect voters, but eligibility was ultimately decided by election officials.

24:10 Operation Eagle Eye: challenging 1.25 million voters nationwide
In the 1964 election, Republicans rolled out "Operation Eagle Eye." Its head, Charles Barr, told media including The New York Times that it expected to challenge or deter 1.25 million voters nationwide. The blueprint was the same as Phoenix: mail into Democratic precincts, and if the mail came back, challenge at the polls. On election day, The New York Times reported Republican officials saying 100,000 trained Republican workers were deployed across 35 key cities. The Miami Herald wrote that "hundreds upon hundreds of voters were confused and frightened into partisan poll-watching." The New York Times said the operation was launched in nearly every state. The FBI was asked to investigate leaflets distributed in Black precincts, whose purpose was to create delay, confusion and fear.

26:12 Goldwater lost; Rehnquist was playing a long game
Rehnquist persuaded Goldwater to oppose and vote against the Civil Rights Act, which became a symbol of Goldwater's extreme conservatism, and even within the party some began to abandon him. But Rehnquist did not. Goldwater was crushed, and Rehnquist wrote his concession speech. The judgment in the episode is: Rehnquist did not care how others saw him, would rather be defeated on an issue than compromise, and believed he could win it back later — he was playing a long game. In 1971, at 47, he was nominated to the Supreme Court, and at his confirmation hearings the voter-suppression allegations did not hold up for lack of evidence. At his 1986 confirmation as chief justice, new witnesses appeared, including former federal assistant attorney general James Brosnahan, but it was still one side's word against the other. He served on the Supreme Court for 33 years, until his death in 2005.

35:30 A neighborhood next to the Ford plant held off bulldozers with a human chain
Ismael Ahmed's father came from Egypt to New York at age 10 on a cargo ship, and no one asked him any questions when he disembarked. In the 1950s the family moved to Detroit, settling in the South End of Dearborn — a narrow strip wedged between the Ford Rouge plant and the city of Detroit. The Rouge plant had 90,000 workers at its peak. In the 1960s, Edward C. Levy Company used Ford waste to make asphalt, and big trucks drove through the neighborhood, spilling waste off open truck beds. After residents protested, the city decided to rezone the neighborhood as heavy industrial, which satisfied Ford and Levy and drove out the people who complained. Arab residents began to fight back: when bulldozers came to tear down houses, women and children formed a human chain in the street. They held on block by block, house by house.

44:58 Wildcat strike: the union bought Israel bonds, and the workers walked
The Arab Workers Caucus discovered that their local UAW had bought more than $300,000 in Israel bonds, and the national union had bought far more. That meant about 15,000 Arab members of the UAW were spending money to support what they saw as a violent occupation. They ran an ad in the Detroit Free Press: these workers viewed the purchase of Israel bonds the way Black workers viewed UAW investment in apartheid South Africa. They petitioned the UAW with no result, then learned that UAW president Leonard Woodcock was to receive an award at a ceremony, and decided to organize a wildcat strike — a strike without union authorization. After more than a month of organizing, on November 28, 1973, about 2,000 workers walked out of the Dodge main plant, not only Arabs but also Black workers. That evening about 1,000 Arabs picketed outside the awards ceremony, and Woodcock slipped in through the back door. The UAW later sold off part of the bonds, though not all of them.

item.title: Fukuyama: The Enemy of Liberal Democracy Isn't Tyranny, It's Boredom
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-oddlots-福山-自由民主的敌人不是专制-是无聊/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-oddlots-福山-自由民主的敌人不是专制-是无聊/
item.description: Nietzsche's "last man" isn't the oppressed — he's the one who's fed, recognized, and no longer wants to strive for anything. Fukuyama thinks that's the real fuel behind today's extremism.
item.content:encoded:
Nietzsche's "last man" isn't the oppressed — he's the one who's fed, recognized, and no longer wants to strive for anything. Fukuyama thinks that's the real fuel behind today's extremism.

Fukuyama himself untangles how "The End of History" was misread, and strings megalothymia, agentic AI and the China model into one line. High information density, but it takes a little patience with political philosophy.

4:08 This discontent runs deeper than the 1930s
Fukuyama doesn't think anyone knows what it means that the AfD won a majority in a local election. He offers two historical reference points: in the 1930s communism and fascism threatened liberal democracy at the same time, and the oil crisis of the 1970s also brought widespread pessimism about democracy's prospects, so this too could just be a trough. But he leans more pessimistic: Freedom House has recorded a global decline in freedom for twenty consecutive years, starting around 2008. The more decisive reason is in the United States — since World War II America has been the model of liberal democracy, and a populist movement rising inside the model country suggests something deeper is going on, not just cyclical fluctuation.

7:14 Love of liberal democracy comes from negative experience
Fukuyama says he didn't anticipate how much generational turnover would matter. For his generation, the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of communism were the defining events, and the driving force behind the essay he wrote on "the end of history." Now it's circling back to the starting point: many of the people who actually lived through those countries want to reverse that outcome. His explanation is that the strongest driver of people valuing liberal democracy is negative experience — living under tyranny. The joy Eastern Europeans felt back then was concrete, because being surveilled and being punished for your speech were real. But the one or two generations that grew up after the Berlin Wall fell don't have that experience, so they easily take peace and prosperity as things that exist by nature, and even see the EU as the world's largest tyranny.

9:17 The end of history isn't my phrase
Fukuyama clarifies: "end of history" is Hegel's wording, and here history is capitalized H, equivalent to what we today call modernization or development; "end" means a goal or endpoint, not "nothing more will happen." The question is: what kind of society will eventually emerge from this long evolution. Marxists took over Hegel's concept of history and said the endpoint is communism; by the late 1980s, Fukuyama judged that communism was out, so the endpoint landed on what communists called bourgeois democracy plus a market economy. He admits the book's choice of words was his own mistake — the real other half is "the last man," from Nietzsche, who detested the idea that history has an endpoint, because the victory of English-style liberalism looked to him like a boring, flat world where everyone is fed and clothed and content, like cattle grazing in a field.

13:19 Liberalism has been accused of eroding community since birth
Fukuyama lays out liberalism's origins very concretely: after the 17th-century European wars of religion, Christians slaughtered each other over transubstantiation, infant baptism and the like, and the early liberals said we have to accept a fact — we don't agree on the highest questions, so let's tolerate each other and live in peace. That is the essence of liberalism: it accepts pluralism and difference. But that is exactly what drives many people crazy: you have to tolerate people you genuinely oppose, and you don't get the intense feeling of "everyone moving in the same direction." Fukuyama says this is where nationalism and religious politics come from. The danger is that people forget what that kind of politics brings — the 20th century was strong national identities asserting themselves and dominating each other, and the result was two world wars; today Putin runs on the same logic, unsatisfied with a peaceful, prosperous Russia and demanding that Ukraine and Belarus be part of it too.

14:20 Billionaires don't want money, they want recognition
Fukuyama uses megalothymia to explain a phenomenon: people aren't satisfied with equal dignity and equal rights, they also want to be recognized as superior. He says this is precisely what Twitter exists for — the richest people in the world still need a platform to be heard and to feel superior. In the original book Fukuyama actually mentioned Donald Trump, framing the benefit of capitalist democracy as a kind of pressure valve: the desire to dominate, to be great, can go straight into making money, and he used Trump as an example, not expecting that money alone wouldn't be enough for him, that he'd also want political glory. Fukuyama doesn't think we can escape megalothymia, because all excellence stems from that will to surpass others; the problem is that it often slides into wanting to be a tyrant. If it stays confined to economic competition, fine, but once it becomes politicized, turns into political ambition, democracy is in trouble.

18:27 Old media had editors; the internet rewards the more extreme
Fukuyama thinks the most dangerous thing digital media does to democracy is that people no longer agree on basic empirical facts. Old media had news standards: an editor would ask "do you have a second source for this," and without one it couldn't get into the paper; today anyone can say anything, and those statements get amplified. He describes an unhealthy dynamic: say something reasonable and sincere and you're immediately sent to the cold palace; once you say something unreasonable, insult people, say absurd and untrue things, your followers surge, and then you have to go further to top the last round. Fukuyama thinks this explains a good deal of the extremism in our politics, because people live in an online world and don't even agree on basic facts anymore.

20:30 The most dangerous thing is handing decisions to machines
Fukuyama says the most dangerous aspect of AI is agentic AI — people delegating decision-making power to machines. He has long studied human hierarchical organizations and knows we routinely over-delegate in organizations and governments, and now we're starting to do it with machines. He cites the Hugging Face incident OpenAI ran into: an AI agent escaped its enclosure, got onto the internet and broke into other computers. The more fundamental problem is that the creators of modern AI don't really understand what's happening underneath — traditional programming executes line by line, highly deterministically, whereas why these new AIs behave the way they do, people can't say. If you delegate power to a machine whose reasoning you don't understand, you're on the road to a genuinely apocalyptic scenario: they behave as if they have their own will, and no one can control them.

24:36 Universal basic income won't fix the dignity problem
Fukuyama doesn't buy the Keynesian optimism — productivity so high that we only need to work ten to twenty hours a week and spend the rest on hobbies. He thinks that ultimately won't make people happy, and the same goes for universal basic income. The reason is thumos: megalothymia comes from this Greek word, meaning spiritedness or pride; beyond material needs, people want their basic dignity recognized. And a good part of dignity comes from what you do — being paid to do a job means someone in society thinks what you do is worth paying for. So a society where everyone sells trinkets on Etsy and no longer does the usual work won't make people happy, because it can't give them pride and a sense of accomplishment. He casually explains why the manosphere is so agitated: online all day, fantasizing that you're a superhero, while in reality knowing it's empty.

item.title: A Bank on Holiday Isn't Inefficient — It's a Fraud Control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-complexsys-银行放假不是效率低-是反内部欺诈的控制手段/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-complexsys-银行放假不是效率低-是反内部欺诈的控制手段/
item.description: When the financial system goes dark on weekends and holidays, it looks like technological backwardness. It's actually a deliberate control: keep the co-conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at once, and the insider fraud surfaces.
item.content:encoded:
When the financial system goes dark on weekends and holidays, it looks like technological backwardness. It's actually a deliberate control: keep the co-conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at once, and the insider fraud surfaces.

Medium information density, with the core insight concentrated in the middle and back half: how holidays get used as anti-fraud controls, and why a 24/7 financial system isn't even logically coherent.

3:29 Holidays are a Schelling point both sides default to
A holiday isn't an authoritative list; it's a Schelling point you and your counterparty default to together. Nobody questions that Christmas is a holiday in the US, so nobody has to ask. But a holiday can also be the product of explicit negotiation: one reason government payroll modernization projects keep failing is that it takes a historian doing a lot of bespoke research to determine which document governs the overtime rate for a Chicago parking enforcement officer on Good Friday. A holiday is both a fact ‘every child knows’ and a negotiable object you can litigate.

6:00 The Bank of Japan's Company Foundation Day is on no official list
The Bank of Japan is also a Japanese company, so some of its human and computer systems rest on days when most office workers are at work, because that day is the bank's own Company Foundation Day. Institutions that interact with it inherit the counterparty's corporate founding anniversary for certain operations. That holiday appears on no list in government publications, Bloomberg, or Google Calendar, yet it carries all the consequences of a holiday. Step on it and the engineering team has to urgently redefine how the system understands global holidays — because when the system asks ‘is today a holiday,’ it usually gets passed a jurisdiction, not a counterparty.

10:33 Black Friday falls inside the four days money doesn't move
Black Friday is the day after Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday follows right behind; transaction volume on those two days spikes as predictably as the sun rising, and they land squarely inside a four-day window when the banking system basically doesn't move money between companies. If you promise a customer ‘we'll pay out the next business day’ while the underlying rail takes two business days to get the money to you, you have a one-day mismatch, and that mismatch consumes float. Normally you only front one day; on a weekend you front three; during BFCM you front about five, including the biggest sales day of the year. That's why hundreds of people spend weeks ahead of time walking through BFCM scenarios, writing contingency plans, and modeling float requirements with finance.

21:29 Crypto tried 24/7, and two banks closing at once broke it
Heavily online technologists hate systems that go down on a predictable schedule, and the crypto crowd especially loves always-on distributed systems with no single point of failure. One idea: have every market participant bank at the same bank, get an internal API for book transfers, and money can move 24/7, with a second bank for redundancy. Crypto did try this road, and then in 2023 discovered just how questionable the design was when two highly correlated banks closed on adjacent weekends at the same time. The lesson: systems that mediate between cultures are useful, and mediating systems frequently need to bridge gaps in operating schedules — a gap you can't eliminate by declaring ‘the only operating schedule is 24/7.’

23:30 Forced vacation exists so conspirators can't assemble
Banks deliberately create misaligned operating schedules; it's an important tool for detecting and containing certain kinds of fraud. The most terrifying fraud comes from insiders who know the back-office processes: a single insider who understands the back office is enough to bring down a bank or cause billions in losses — Barings and Daiwa in '95, Société Générale in '08, UBS in '11 are all examples. A very old control is forced vacation, whose purpose is to keep the group involved in a conspiracy from assembling enough co-conspirators, in the right place on the right day, all sitting at the keyboard at once. So a finance CEO sleeping on a beanbag chair in the office may be very dedicated, but both the company and he himself had better not allow it.

26:31 Expecting the financial system to be always-on isn't even self-consistent
In a world that's ever more interconnected, where decision-makers increasingly prize nines, it's reasonable to expect the financial system to partly narrow the gap between historical and contemporary practice. Culture creates systems, and systems create culture; both change, and infrastructure changes far more slowly than fashion, but it does change. Still, expecting the financial system to run continuously isn't just something you shouldn't expect — it isn't even a self-consistent expectation: the financial system is a nested network of organizations, systems, and subsystems, resting at bottom on individuals who have been made complex sociocultural promises and who have a physiological need for sleep. Those people will keep resting and celebrating periodically, just as they keep working for the society the financial system supports.

item.title: The Houthis seize the second strait, and $100 oil is just the start
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-indicator-胡塞武装掐住第二个海峡-油价破百只是开始/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-indicator-胡塞武装掐住第二个海峡-油价破百只是开始/
item.description: Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered. Now the Houthis have taken Perim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, and Saudi Arabia's alternative export route around Hormuz is in doubt too.
item.content:encoded:
Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered. Now the Houthis have taken Perim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, and Saudi Arabia's alternative export route around Hormuz is in doubt too.

Eight minutes to explain why a strait most people have never heard of suddenly matters, with concrete mechanics and numbers. Good for a commute.

2:00 The Red Sea is not just another waterway
In normal, calm times, nearly 15% of global seaborne trade passes through the Red Sea, including 30% of global container shipping, 12% of seaborne oil trade and 8% of liquefied natural gas. At its northern end the Red Sea connects to Egypt and the Suez Canal, and on to the Mediterranean; at its southern end that narrow channel leading to the Indian Ocean and Asian trade routes is the Bab-el-Mandeb. To grasp the weight of this strait, you first have to grasp how much the Red Sea itself carries — it is not a bypass you can casually route around, but a segment of the global trade trunk line.

3:05 The Houthis really did take the ground
The host pressed Rachel on whether "seem to have seized" was hedging, and Rachel confirmed it: the Houthis are a rebel group that has gradually taken control of large parts of Yemen since at least 2014, allied with Iran, and strongly opposed to Israel's existence and to how Israel is fighting in Gaza. In November 2023 they began attacking Red Sea shipping, hijacking vessels and striking with drones and missiles; the US military responded with bombing, and the Red Sea was relatively calm for a while. But over the weekend they moved, seizing a stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast, possibly to support Iran.

4:09 Perim Island is the key that pinches the strait
The seized stretch includes an island right in the middle of the Bab-el-Mandeb — Perim Island (Barim Island), which the military calls "key terrain" because it overlooks the entire strait, and the strait is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point. Whoever controls that chokepoint decides which ships get through. Red Sea traffic had already slowed because of the Houthi attacks, initially falling 50%, and it never fully recovered. Now that Perim Island has been taken, the threat is that this route shuts down entirely.

4:09 Saudi Arabia's way around Hormuz is in doubt too
This is a particularly thorny problem for Saudi Arabia. After Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz more than six months ago, Saudi Arabia had been treating the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb as an alternative oil export route, sending oil through an east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports for loading. But last week that Saudi Red Sea pipeline was hit by drones, and Saudi Arabia then suspended oil loadings from one Red Sea port. Rachel says this puts even more pressure on this lifeline for Saudi Arabia and for the global economy — the creative workaround meant to cushion the world economy is itself extremely fragile.

5:10 Schrodinger Strait: you can collect without firing a shot
The Houthis could close the Bab-el-Mandeb at any time, but so far they haven't. Rachel says the mere fact that they can is itself having an effect. Analysts call it the "Schrodinger Strait" — is it open or closed? That uncertainty alone pushes up insurance costs, pushes up freight rates, and adds friction to the global economy. After news of the Houthi advance last week, oil prices briefly spiked above $100 a barrel.

6:10 Refined products are rising faster than crude
Rachel points out that timing is critical: global supply gaps were already accumulating, only partly offset by rerouting and releases from strategic petroleum reserves, while refineries are seeing severe outages. That means not only are crude prices rising, but diesel, gasoline and other petroleum products are rising proportionally more, because getting refined products to market has become harder. And it isn't just oil products — this strait also carries fertilizer and natural gas, which would be a problem if Europe gets a cold winter.

7:10 Sulfur and helium: the overlooked knock-on shortages
Sulfur is a byproduct of natural gas and fuel production, its supply is already more constrained, and it is used in metal processing, including copper. Helium is a byproduct of natural gas deposits, used as an input in semiconductors and in various medical devices. Countries including the US and Canada are ramping up production of some of these goods, offsetting part of the price increase, but Rachel says not by much. That means shortages from this new trade disruption will reach ordinary people before long.

7:10 US consumers end up footing the bill
Rachel says Americans should care because these are global markets, and you can't build a wall and stop importing. Some US producers may benefit from shortages, but in this scenario US consumers tend to be the ones who lose. She also warns that it isn't just higher prices to worry about: the Houthi actions, plus Iran's refusal to yield, are straining relations among regional countries and between the US and its Middle East allies. Deteriorating US relations with its allies could make other US policy goals harder to achieve — Gulf states, for instance, are major investors in the US and key to US onshore production.

item.title: Clovis People Didn't Just Hunt Mammoths — They Painted and Sewed in Tents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/
item.description: Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles unearthed at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.
item.content:encoded:
Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles unearthed at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.

High density of archaeological detail, but it demands patience: the first half is Clovis research history and dating debates, the second half — the concrete finds at LaPrele — is the part that's really worth your time.

3:02 Clovis lasted only a few hundred years
Radiocarbon dating pins Clovis culture to roughly 13,100 to 12,750 years ago — a window of a few hundred years just before the end of the Ice Age. The narrowness of that span is itself startling: the Ice Age operates on scales of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, and Clovis is just a brief instant within it. More crucially, within those few hundred years, highly similar fluted stone projectile points appeared across the entire North American continent, from New Mexico to Wyoming, from Washington State to Virginia. This combination of "narrow in time, wide in space" is Clovis's most distinctive feature; in later periods, projectile points rapidly regionalized.

12:21 Clovis were not the first Americans
The "Clovis First" theory dominated most of the 20th century: humans followed mammoth herds into the Americas, and Clovis people were the earliest settlers. But finds at sites like Monte Verde (Chile), Paisley Caves (Oregon), Cooper's Ferry (Idaho) and Page-Ladson (Florida) have led most archaeologists to now believe people were living in the Americas thousands of years before Clovis. Mackey says this is one of the fiercest debates in American archaeology, with Pleistocene archaeologists arguing bitterly over it. But she also stresses: Clovis research shouldn't fixate only on the question of "who came first" — there are many questions worth asking about their lives themselves.

21:01 One chopper changed the entire nature of the site
The LaPrele site was discovered in 1986 when locals found mammoth bones by a creek; Mackey and collaborators returned to excavate in the 2000s. In the first season, retired archaeologist Rich Adams, while helping everyone fix the screening channel, found a large chopper about 10 meters from the mammoth — a simple tool made by knocking a few flakes off a river cobble. The key point is that it appeared in a position where it geologically shouldn't: the site was gradually buried by floods, and natural processes were unlikely to have moved such a large cobble there. This tool prompted the team to test a wider area, ultimately finding over 50,000 flakes, at least four artifact concentration areas, several hundred stone tools and mammoth ivory. LaPrele was no longer just a kill site, but a camp where humans had lived.

29:15 Hearths and tent walls left fingerprints in the sediment
LaPrele's most striking find is four "hearth-centered areas." In Block B, the team found no obvious ash or oxidation traces, but burned bone and flakes concentrated in a small area, indicating a hearth once stood there. Even more compelling is the spatial analysis: if you look down from above at a tent, the hearth is at the center, surrounded by a high-activity zone, then an open space for walking, and near the tent wall objects accumulate — because the wall is a barrier to artifact transport. Block B's artifact distribution shows exactly this "bullseye" pattern, indicating an indoor space. In the same area, a roughly 1.5-by-2-meter scatter of ochre (hematite) pigment was found, matching the wall's position, suggesting people painted by the fire.

39:25 The bone needles were made from red fox and felid bone
The team used ZooMS (Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry) to analyze bone needles and possible bone beads; this method extracts proteins from extremely small bone samples to identify the animal species. The results were unexpected: many needles were made from hare bone, but one was red fox, and another tested as felid — not a domestic cat, but some wild felid. Mackey notes these are all fur-bearing animals, and their bone thickness may have been just right for making needles. More importantly, these animals were likely caught in traps rather than hunted with spears. This means Clovis people weren't hunting mammoths 24 hours a day — they were also taking more common small prey.

44:32 Were Clovis people mammoth specialists or omnivores?
About 15 widely accepted Clovis sites in North America coexist with megafauna, mostly proboscideans (mammoth, mastodon, gomphothere), but also horse and camel. Yet Mackey points out that only about 30 to 40 sites truly define our understanding of Clovis, while thousands of Clovis projectile points were found on the surface, lacking context. This raises a core debate: were they mammoth-hunting specialists, or omnivores with a broader diet? Small animals, fish and plant remains preserve less easily and are less often systematically sought. Mackey is studying plant remains, and she notes archaeologists usually look for plants only in hearths — and how many places in the Clovis record have actually been searched is a problem.

50:00 Mammoth extinction: did humans push, or was climate the main driver?
The classic "overkill" debate: 35 genera of megafauna went extinct at the end of the Ice Age — how much was human versus environmental? Mackey says she takes a middle path, believing both contributed. She considers mammoths the strongest candidate for the overkill hypothesis, because mammoth sites are numerous, the animals were large, and their reproductive rate was low, making them more vulnerable to hunting. But she also notes overkill doesn't necessarily mean humans hunted all 35 genera — hunting may have tipped the balance through trophic cascades. Interestingly, paleoecologists lean toward "humans did it," while archaeologists lean more toward "the environment did it."

53:12 Clovis human bone barely exists
Apart from a single ancestral remain attributed to Clovis at the Anzick site in Montana, we have almost no Clovis human bone. Mackey doesn't find this surprising: population density was extremely low, 13,000-year-old sites are inherently extremely hard to preserve, and these groups were highly mobile, so we don't know their burial practices. She also stresses that Clovis people are the ancestors of millions of Indigenous people in the Americas today, and any related research must proceed on the basis of consultation and collaboration.

item.title: 40,000 Ottomans Lay Siege to Malta — and Lose to a Few Hundred Knights
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-historyhit-奥斯曼四万大军围攻马耳他-为何败给几百骑士/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-historyhit-奥斯曼四万大军围攻马耳他-为何败给几百骑士/
item.description: In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the delay lasted until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.
item.content:encoded:
In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the delay lasted until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.

This episode is on-location siege narrative — vivid but light on analysis. If you want the mechanics of why Malta held, the middle and later sections on scorched earth and disinformation are the most valuable.

3:02 Malta's value is its position, not its resources
Malta sits almost exactly in the middle of the Mediterranean: 80 km north of Sicily, hard against North Africa to the south, and roughly equidistant from Gibraltar and the Suez Canal. Whoever controls Malta controls the trade routes. The Grand Harbour, where Valletta now stands, is a rare natural deep-water port that is safe to anchor in whatever direction the wind blows. The Knights did not initially want Malta, since it had no ready-made fortifications and no resources; it was the first Grand Master who insisted on a foothold and took it.

7:10 What the Knights brought was the Italian bastion
The Knights brought Italian-style military architecture (Traccia Italiana) to Malta: no longer the tall medieval castle, but low, sloped, outward-projecting bastions with thick walls packed with earth to absorb the impact of gunpowder artillery. Fort St Angelo got the first bastion. By 1552 the Knights had realised how dangerous their position was, and the Grand Master Domades pushed hard to build fortifications. An underwater iron chain was also strung between St Angelo and Fort St Michael at Senglea, serving much like a WWII anti-submarine net to block ships.

11:26 The defenders were waiting for a fleet on the horizon
On 18 May 1565 the garrison of Fort St Elmo saw a vast fleet approaching on the horizon, signalled at once, and the whole island went to war footing. The defenders numbered about 10,000 in total, including knights, Maltese civilians and mercenaries hired from Italy. This was not a war you could surrender in: the defeated would be killed or sold as slaves, so for many it was a fight to the death. The Ottomans, for their part, arrived thinking they would take it in a few days and move on to the next place, and set their first objective on Fort St Elmo.

13:33 Fort St Elmo held only a month, but it tied the Ottomans down
The Ottoman fleet of about 190 ships and an estimated 35,000 soldiers arrived at the Grand Harbour and did not strike directly at the Knights' headquarters at Fort St Angelo, but first attacked Fort St Elmo, which guarded the two harbour entrances. Fire opened on 27 May, with hundreds of guns bombarding almost without pause and reducing the walls to rubble; every night the Knights patched the breaches, hauled ammunition and tended the wounded, then fought again the next day. Fort St Elmo had been thrown up in only about six months, its works were not good enough, and the Ottomans found it relatively easy to scale and dismantle. The Grand Master's strategy was simply to keep the Ottomans attacking and keep bleeding them. By the night of 22 June the fort was a ruin, and the surviving defenders said Mass in the chapel, preparing not for victory but for death. At noon on 23 June the last knights died fighting and Fort St Elmo fell.

16:46 Both sides used corpses to send a message
This was a war with no room for surrender. After the last defenders of Fort St Elmo were killed, the Ottomans cut off their heads and lashed the bodies to rafts in the shape of a cross, casting them into the sea as a warning to the Grand Master of what was coming. The Grand Master is said to have fired the Ottomans' heads back from the guns of Fort St Angelo in reply. On 15 July the Ottomans tried to attack Senglea, but below Fort St Angelo at sea level there was a small battery the Ottomans had not spotted; when it opened fire they were caught completely off guard, and nearly all the attacking boats were sunk.

18:51 Scorched earth left the Ottomans unable to hold out
By July the Knights' side still had reasonable supplies; it was the Ottomans who were in trouble. The Knights and the Maltese practised scorched earth, burning everything as they withdrew, so the Ottomans could find no food. It was high summer and the heat was punishing, and Ottoman morale began to sink into panic. The Grand Master's tactic was to wear down the enemy's manpower and morale as much as possible and drag things out until they gave up on their own. An Ottoman leader is said to have remarked that if St Elmo had taken this long, what would St Angelo cost. Maltese civilians also fought in large numbers, including women who took part in nursing and in combat.

22:03 A tiny cavalry force scared off an Ottomans army on the brink of victory
In early August the Ottomans attacked both Birgu and Senglea at once, at one point breaking through the walls and fighting hand to hand in the streets, and they looked to have the upper hand. The Knights countered with a ruse: a commander at Mdina, the fortified city in the Maltese interior, sent out a very small force of Maltese cavalry, which raided the Ottoman field hospital and supply camp. Rumour spread fast through the Ottoman army that a huge relief force had arrived. The Ottoman commander Mustafa Pasha broke off the assault, retreating on the edge of victory. By the end of August both sides were locked in a war of attrition, with disease, lack of food and casualties mounting, and the Ottomans had also lost experienced commanders such as Dragut.

23:03 The relief came, but the Ottoman Empire was not broken
On 7 September 1565, 8,000 Spanish, Italian and Sicilian troops sent by Don Garcia in the name of Philip II of Spain landed on Malta from Sicily and advanced on the exhausted Ottoman army. The Knights had been begging for help for weeks, and the relief was late but it came. The Ottomans formally surrendered. But Kirsty stresses that this did not weaken the Ottoman Empire's power or legitimacy; it continued as an empire for a long time afterwards, and today people tend to inflate the significance of this victory. After the siege the Knights immediately set about building the new city of Valletta and repairing Fort St Elmo; the Grand Master La Valette died before he saw the city finished.

item.title: Australia Regulates Supplements Like Drugs, but Nobody Checks Whether They Work
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.description: Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested during production — the impression of "good" was planted by marketing and cross-border policy.
item.content:encoded:
Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested during production — the impression of "good" was planted by marketing and cross-border policy.

The first half's regulatory breakdown is solid, and the back half's chain from marketing to daigou policy is complete; but the middle section has a lot of transcription garbage, so the information density is uneven.

4:00 Australians taking pills is a tradition, not a climate
The soil for Australia's supplement industry isn't the natural environment, it's four social habits: a sparse population that encourages self-medication, pharmacists who also diagnose and dispense, a naturopathy industry body dating to the 1920s, and health food stores resembling food-as-medicine shops. Stacked together, these four made Australians used to "solving health problems without going to the hospital." Black Moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathy clinic; only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognise — turning "take a spoonful of fish oil a day" into standardised fish oil capsules.

12:05 The contract manufacturers are the industry's foundation
Pen Pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was Australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing of supplements, and by around 2003 it was producing roughly 70% of Australia's vitamins, minerals and herbal products. Its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, the oil-and-gelatin seal of soft capsules, the mixing uniformity of powders, the stability of liquids — each is its own set of solutions. In the 1980s and 90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended service in both directions, moving from pure production (CMO) to CDMO covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labelling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. The brand only has to hand over a concept, and the factory can turn it into a product ready to sell.

15:05 Registration means nobody looks before it hits the shelf
Australia legislated in 1989, putting the TGA in charge of both pharmaceuticals and supplements, and all products must obtain an AUST number. Most supplements fall into the AUSTL category: only low-risk ingredients permitted by the TGA, only low-level health claims, and companies get a number just by applying themselves — the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. By around 2010 Australia had roughly ten thousand complementary medicines, of which nearly 98% were in this registration system. Only prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the AUSTR tier, which requires the TGA to assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.

20:06 It looks strict, but in practice it is loose
Put contract manufacturing and regulation together and you see that GMP only guarantees the factory produces consistently to the standard the brand gives it, and that problems can be traced to a batch recall — it is not itself responsible for whether the product works. The TGA side only handles declarations and issuing batch numbers; efficacy is explained by the brand itself. So the claim that "Australia regulates supplements like drugs" is not wrong, but it is misleading: the method of control is the same, but the degree of control over the efficacy part differs enormously. The whole system does no effective upfront oversight of a product's actual effect, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and the product's efficacy.

25:08 The marketing was copied from Centrum, not invented
CEO Radek Sali, who took over in 2008, did not conjure a marketing plan out of thin air. He did industry research and found that the best-selling peer was Centrum, and feedback from retailers was: Centrum didn't give the channel much profit, but it was on TV all year round with heavy advertising and good athlete endorsements, and consumers would ask for it by name when they walked into a pharmacy. Sali wanted to replicate this at Swisse. He first invested in Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's team captain, buying only very short ad slots during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so that even a limited budget could appear at important moments. But the female-dominated sales channel wasn't impressed; one buyer didn't watch cricket herself and didn't know the athlete. He asked his mother what shows she liked, and she said a dance variety show, and the strategy pivoted to spoken-word placements in entertainment content.

26:09 Selling health as a lifestyle
Swisse's bigger promotional push drew on Oprah and Ellen, and signed actress Nicole Kidman for three years, extending its reach from Australia to the US. By 2012 Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, and reached annual revenue of 183 million Australian dollars, with marketing spend of 40 to 50 million Australian dollars a year — reportedly at one point the highest marketing spend of any consumer brand in Australia. Its ads didn't emphasise efficacy or ingredients; they mainly presented a state of being energetic, self-disciplined and good-looking — turning health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse took more than 20% market share in Australian supermarkets and more than 10% in pharmacies.

32:14 The growth engine was found in Chinese pharmacies
Swisse's expensive push into the US market wasn't a success, and on returning to Australia it found that Swisse sold extremely well in pharmacies in Chinese-populated areas — some stores sold at ten times the level of ordinary stores — because students and Chinese immigrants bought in bulk to take back to China or resell online, i.e. daigou. Two policy shifts came in 2015: in March the Hangzhou cross-border e-commerce comprehensive pilot zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement, which took effect in December that year. The FTA mainly affected ordinary trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average of 20%, and after the agreement it was said the rate could fall to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce went through bonded warehouses, platforms bought in bulk, logistics time and cost fell sharply, and such goods were treated in policy as for personal use, so they didn't have to go through the registration and filing process for supplement imports.

35:16 The brand was bought; the impression stayed put
In September 2015, Hong Kong-listed Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full buyout, at a deal size of about 1.7 billion Australian dollars, or 8.7 billion RMB. For Swisse the deal carried little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. Now all those Swisse ads on Hunan TV variety shows are, in theory, a Chinese supplement company spending money, yet the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still apply their old vague good impression of Australia to it — the core value of the acquisition rests, in large proportion, in brand goodwill.

item.title: Lenin Built the Terror Machine; Stalin Just Took It Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.description: The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.
item.content:encoded:
The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.

This episode gets the attribution of the Soviet terror system straight: it wasn't invented out of thin air by Stalin, it was a stage built by Lenin on which Stalin performed. The back half, on Lenin's testament and the funeral details, is dense with information.

2:06 In 1917 Stalin was a man nobody noticed
The episode opens by recalling the impression left by the previous instalment: Stalin was a bad orator and a slow theorist, and nobody would have guessed he was the next dictator. Guest Giles Milton confirms that judgement and adds a key detail — Stalin rarely appeared in public and was not well known in Russia; he hated public speaking because his Georgian accent was so thick. This explains how he was later able to accumulate power quietly: nobody treated him as a threat.

4:11 Churchill once wanted to wipe out the Red Army with gas
During the civil war, Britain, France, the US and Japan all backed the Whites. Churchill, as Minister of Munitions in 1919, pushed Britain to send troops and weapons to Russia to fight the Reds. More striking still, Britain had developed a lethal chemical weapon late in the First World War, and Churchill thought it more humane than the bloody slaughter in the trenches, so he sent it to use against Trotsky's Red Army. Because of the atmospheric conditions in northern Russia the gas worked poorly, and the whole stock was eventually dumped into the White Sea. This history explains how hard it was when Churchill allied with Stalin in 1941 — he himself was one of the men who had wanted to get rid of Stalin back then.

9:27 The terror machine's architecture was Lenin's legacy
Many people put the Cheka, the labour camps and the one-party system all down to Stalin, saying he built them while serving as a political commissar in the civil war. Giles argues this is a complete misreading of Lenin's role: it was Lenin who built this architecture, and Stalin merely took it later and used it for his own political career. The Cheka was the secret police, which later became the more familiar KGB — surveillance, arrest, torture, execution. The host sums it up: when we look back at history we often say Stalin was a corrosive influence, that he brought the terror, but the architecture was in fact Lenin's bequest.

10:27 Tsaritsyn: Stalin arrested a front-line general
Trotsky appointed Snezarev, a general from the former tsarist army, to command the Tsaritsyn campaign — a typical Trotsky move of using old officers, and one that put him directly at odds with Stalin. Stalin, as political commissar, arrested the general and all his subordinate officers and locked them on a barge on the Volga. It is said his intention was to sink the boat and drown them. When Trotsky found out he was furious and ordered the general released immediately. This was the first round in the struggle between Trotsky and Stalin, and Trotsky won it decisively. But Stalin later told the story as one of the great civil-war battles in which he personally went to the front, and Tsaritsyn was later renamed Stalingrad.

16:44 Whenever Stalin was unhappy he threatened to resign
Giles tells a detail that does not fit Stalin's later image: whenever things went badly, for instance when he was not authorised at Tsaritsyn to settle scores with Trotsky, he threatened to resign. He wrote a letter saying that without this, his work on the Southern Front would become meaningless and unnecessary, and that this gave him the right or the obligation to go even to the devil rather than remain on the Southern Front. The Politburo read the letter, grew weary of it, and said, no, Joseph, stay, we all love you. He was a sulker. The picture fixes in the reader's mind that the early Stalin used emotional blackmail, not terror.

29:12 Nobody at the time wanted the job of General Secretary
In April 1922 Stalin was appointed General Secretary. Today the title means supreme power in the state, but at the time it was just a functional description, tedious work. Stalin understood: handled properly, the post gave him complete control of the party. He could plant his own people in key positions and clear out everyone who supported Trotsky. From the day he took over he made full use of the position, and already had one eye on the future — Lenin's health was poor, he was thinking about who would succeed Lenin, and now he had the chance to fill the party with supporters so that when Lenin died he would be in an advantageous position.

32:13 Stalin's apology letter: says sorry without admitting fault
Stalin telephoned Lenin's household. Lenin was gravely ill, and Stalin accused Nadezhda of discussing politics with Lenin as he was dying, saying it was unforgivable. Nadezhda told Lenin, Lenin was furious, and insisted Stalin write a letter of apology. The letter is superb: Stalin apologises without apologising — if you think I offended her, then I apologise, but I do not think I really offended her, so there is nothing to apologise for. Lenin was even angrier. On 4 January 1923 Lenin wrote down his assessment of Stalin: Stalin is too rude, and this defect, entirely tolerable in our internal and comradely relations, becomes intolerable in the post of General Secretary, and he therefore proposed that the comrades find a way to remove Stalin and replace him with someone else.

35:21 If Lenin had not died, Stalin would have put him in prison
Lenin's political life ended with his stroke, and he died ten days later. His wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, said the most famous line of all: if Lenin had not died in 1924, he would have been serving time in one of Stalin's prisons. She saw that Stalin had turned on Lenin as he rose. Giles thinks it very likely, because Stalin was absolutely ruthless towards anyone he believed was not on his side. Lenin wanted a simple burial; Stalin decided not to bury him but to embalm and preserve him and put him on permanent display. Within hours of Lenin's death they began draining his fluids and removing his organs, and the heart was never found again.

item.title: The Solo Founder Isn't Alone: The Relationship Is the Product
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
