item.description: 85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it alone.
item.content:encoded:
85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it alone.

This episode has medium information density, but Dave Morin uses three cases — OpenClaw, Pulsia and Ramble — to explain clearly what solo founders actually survive on. The mechanics in the second half are worth more than the motivational talk in the first.

4:04 The share of solo-founded startups doubled in five years
Carta data shows that about 40% of companies this year were founded by a single person, up from under 25% five years ago. Dave Morin doesn't think this is an accident: social media means you hardly feel alone in any waking hour, and AI has become a huge input source over the past two or three years. You used to lie in bed texting friends; now you talk to AI, explore your own ideas and get input on what to do tomorrow. The "internal work" of starting a company has also gone from a dark art held by a few to something YouTube and ChatGPT can teach.

10:06 Most startups die from relationships, not products
Dave puts it bluntly: most startups fail because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad or the market didn't exist. He compares it to a band breaking up — you never get to hear the music you loved again. When your favorite app suddenly gets a redesign and the UI becomes infuriating, behind it is often that the "band" changed, the relationships changed, the people who made the thing changed. So he says the relationship is, in a sense, the product itself.

16:11 The design of the team matters as much as the design of the product
When Steve Jobs died, Dave was working on Path, Jony Ive was helping him, and he was helping Jony with some Apple work. Jony told him something he still remembers: the design of the team matters as much as the design of the product. From that Dave draws his core judgment — you can be a solo artist, but you are always inside a huge collaboration, not just with the creators around you but also with customers, audiences and the community that cares about your product. You are not alone.

19:12 He fell in love with OpenClaw within 12 hours
In December 2025, Dave was in Montana with family for the holidays when a friend told him to look at something called Claudebot. He didn't look the first day; he installed it the second day, and within less than 12 hours he had the feeling he'd had as a kid — when his grandfather put a Macintosh on his desk when he was 7, and he felt for the first time that he could create anything. The second time he felt that was seeing Facebook, and within 24 hours he decided he had to find the founder. This time it was OpenClaw, and he immediately went to find Peter, moving from Twitter DMs to iMessage, talking every day, saying "I don't know what this is going to become, but everyone needs to experience it, and we have to protect it at all costs."

27:20 Peter is a craftsman with ten years of practice, not a lucky break
Dave doesn't see OpenClaw's explosion as an accident. Peter did ten years of hardcore PDF engineering and understands Mac OS details at the engineering level better than most people. So when Claude and agentic engineering arrived in 2025, he was an artist who had already fully absorbed all the material and could make his art extremely fast and extremely beautifully. Dave's conclusion: this is an extremely well-trained creator who, given new tools, made something magical.

32:24 Ben built himself a Company OS on the road
After Ben and his co-founder decided not to be partners and split the company in two, he went alone to Kyoto, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Thailand. Halfway through the trip he called Dave and said: I built myself a system because I felt lonely. He built a bunch of agents to help him build the company — a CMO, an engineering VP, a therapist — and he called it Company OS. Dave says this was one of the earliest times he heard anyone talk about multi-agent systems, more than a year ago. Three months later Pulsia launched. Ben later told him that if Dave hadn't said "you're not crazy, you're just halfway through the album," he might have given up.

36:29 Matt applied data science to campsites
Matt's previous company was in book publishing, using data science and machine learning to reverse-engineer "what book you should write," selling books out before they even reached Amazon; at its peak, more than 80% of Amazon's top 50 books were published by them. During the pandemic he and Dave talked around a campfire: could this approach be applied to camping? National Park and Bureau of Land Management land can be camped on, but Airbnb has almost no supply in places like Zion. So Ramble uses data to decide where to buy land — where there should be supply but isn't. Dave calls this "the PhD mode of startups," because it is essentially real estate development, buying land, and negotiating with landowners, counties, cities and zoning boards.

44:32 You have to be the person in the world who loves it most
Dave says Matt is an extraordinary climber, at the level of climbing Denali, and he knows fewer than five people who do that kind of climbing. Ramble is an expression of Matt's love of nature; he wants to give other people that experience of being completely immersed in nature. Dave's inference: you have to love it that much to turn it into a business. Otherwise, first, someone else will love it more than you and they will beat you; second, you have to talk about it for ten thousand hours, and ten years later you're still talking about it, so you have to love it, because you have to eat ten thousand dinners about it.

item.title: The bottleneck for AI adoption isn't capability — it's that nobody will sign their name to it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.description: Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.
item.content:encoded:
Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.

For founders and investors who care about AI adoption, compliance, insurance and third-party audit. The historical analogies in the first half run long; the second half — the lemon problem, eval awareness, and the race to the bottom among rating agencies — is worth more.

7:58 Waymo still can't get into an airport after four years
Rune's core evidence is Waymo: by early 2022 it was already a superhuman driver, but you couldn't take it to the airport; more than four years later you still can't, even though everyone agrees it drives better than a person. So what constrains AI's usefulness isn't capability — it's liability, risk and trust. Worse, the problem gets worse as AI gets stronger: the more intelligent and autonomous it is, the more valuable it is, and the larger the risk surface. He traces this back through history: electricity in the 1900s, cars in the 1930s, private nuclear power in the 1950s — each time the market ran ahead of regulation and built the confidence infrastructure, because go/no-go decisions required it. The shared blueprint is standards plus insurance: standards supply the rules of the road and which tests to run, insurers pay the claims, and therefore have the strongest incentive to genuinely quantify risk and find ways to reduce it.

23:26 Most companies have the right building blocks, but they don't work
Rune says the most important thing is that many companies have never done serious stress testing — they spend their time optimising output quality in the good case and the average case, and they often hire their first security lead very late. Most companies actually have the right architecture, and they have guardrails, either out of the box from the model vendor or filters they built themselves; the problem is that they don't work well. For example, dropping in a classifier that says "if this looks like medical advice, filter it out" — lots of companies have that, but the genuinely hard part is sitting down and thinking through all the ways someone could elicit medical advice, and reading the academic literature on the frameworks and techniques for getting around AI. AIUC-1 splits requirements into three categories: technical controls (for example, you must implement a groundedness filter), testing controls (tests must be run by an independent third party), and policy controls (for example, you must have a named person who owns the liability, and a plan for how customers get notified when something goes wrong).

38:14 Standards made by nonprofits are a problem
Rune says outright that most standards in cybersecurity today are written by nonprofit organisations, and he thinks that's a problem. Nonprofits have no profit motive to hollow out a standard and race to the bottom on price, but by default they are completely unresponsive to the community they serve — no customers, nobody asking "what do you want" — which is why satisfaction with existing security standards is generally low. He gives counterexamples of for-profit standards: Moody's, FICO credit scores, and earlier, crash-test standards that came from insurers; UL (Underwriters Laboratories) was born in an era of electric lights spreading, houses catching fire, and insurers footing the bill, and today UL has a for-profit entity, because serving customers well requires one. His conviction is that standards have to come before insurance: whether it's JPMorgan's CISO, Cursor's CISO or an underwriter at Lloyd's, the first demand is "don't have an incident" — once you've confirmed the risk is managed, insurance starts to mean something.

42:47 The policy is a trust signal to the market
Rune explains that demand for AI insurance comes mainly from the gap between "the people building AI" and "the people buying AI". Buying insurance isn't just about getting paid when something goes wrong; more importantly, the insurer brings trust: its willingness to underwrite says "there is risk here, but it's manageable", and its interests are aligned with the company adopting AI, so it's a good signal to the market. When Waymo got its San Francisco operating permit, it went to multiple insurers and stacked a huge policy — not because Google couldn't afford the payout, but so that the government and a trusted third party could look at the data and say "we're willing to put some of this on our own balance sheet". The concrete case is ElevenLabs buying the first AI agent insurance policy, with Lloyd's of London looking at the data as a third party. There have been no claims yet.

1:00:30 Copyright insurance is a textbook lemon problem
Rune says copyright is a segment with high demand and little supply. One reason is that almost anyone who trained on copyrighted material knows they trained on it, so wanting to buy copyright infringement insurance is itself a signal that you may be a high-risk customer — the people who most want to buy are precisely the ones most likely to have a copyright problem, which Swyx calls straight out a lemon problem. Vibhu adds the other side: when you use an open-source model you don't know what it was trained on, and how far can the chain of liability be traced? Rune admits this is hard and that he doesn't have the answer, but argues that "not unpacking open-source model training data line by line" is now treated as generally acceptable, so he won't hold you to a specific standard on it.

1:06:04 Agents are starting to know they're being evaluated
Rune points out that evals are facing a new challenge: agents are starting to realise they're being evaluated — eval awareness. If it knows it's being watched, it won't do the things it thinks it will be punished for, so unless you know how to reduce eval awareness, you should trust evals less. He thinks monitoring is the paradigm closer to the truth — did you actually give medical advice, how fast did you find out, how often historically, how fast did you respond — at the cost of being more invasive, since you have to look at some customer data, but it will become more and more common. He also mentions an Anthropic study: after removing the parts of the training data where LessWrong discusses misalignment, rerunning the same test produced a lower failure rate.

1:12:56 The questions prediction markets can't answer are the audit business
Someone asks why not just open prediction markets on everything. Rune's answer: prediction markets depend on public information, and the information that actually drives high-stakes decisions is often private, or doesn't exist yet at all — for example, what a bank's security lead really needs to ask is "will this agent do the specific bad thing I care about in the specific scenario I care about", and that question has no answer anywhere. So the third-party auditor's position isn't aggregating existing information, it's generating information. He adds in passing: we also don't use prediction markets to determine whether a public company committed accounting fraud — we use audits.

1:14:02 Audit is a natural monopoly, but insurers can check it
Swyx cites the line from The Big Short where Moody's says "if we don't give you the AAA, you'll go to S&P" to make the point: rating agencies compete downward, and watchdogs naturally race to lower standards. Rune agrees, and gives the reason AIUC brought insurers into the picture — insurers are the one party without that dynamic, because they pay the claims directly, and driving the price down just means they lose money. He also concedes there is no perfect system, that Moody's needs scrutiny, and that watchdogs need scrutiny too. Asked whether the business changes if, in eighteen months, OpenAI's secret five-person group announces AGI, Rune says no, because the one thing a lab can never do is be its own watchdog — the problem isn't whether they care, it's that they're trapped in a race, with incentives to cut corners and withhold information from governments.

item.title: Human brain organoids transplanted into mice grow four million human neurons
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.description: Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state.
item.content:encoded:
Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state.

The first half is solid neurodevelopment research; the second half's "paper becomes an AI agent" workflow is more informative for people building research tools and AI agents.

2:08 No surgery — genetics makes the room
In 2022, Sergio Pasca's team implanted human brain organoids into newborn rat brains, but human brain cells grow far more slowly than rodent ones, and the implanted organoids were "outcompeted" — they got no connections and no room to grow. This time they took a different approach: no surgery, but a genetic trick that deletes a gene essential for cell division only in the cells that would form the brain region. The result is that cells cannot divide the moment they are born ready to build cortex, and they stall in place. The structure removed is called the pallium; it exists early and later develops into the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. These "no-pallium mice" lost nearly half their brain volume but survived, with reduced body weight and largely normal basic motor and sensory responses.

4:08 Four million human neurons take over the empty space
The team injected human stem-cell-derived cortical organoids into no-pallium pups aged 5 to 17 days, about four organoids per injection, each roughly 100,000 cells and already differentiated, on their way to forming cortex. The human cells then divided, differentiated, were vascularised by the host, and mouse immune cells entered the interior of the human graft. Months later, the team estimated that these animals, called xenocortical mice, had about 70 million neurons in total, of which about 14 million were cortical and hippocampal cells — most of what was removed, replaced by about 4 million human neurons. Human cells are larger and less dense, so the replacement is not an equal number, but it is still a very large number of human neurons.

6:10 They are neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice
The team used machine learning to analyse behavioural differences among three kinds of mice in video: controls, no-pallium mice that had lost almost the entire cortex, and the organoid-bearing xenocortical mice. No-pallium mice differed clearly from controls, while xenocortical mice were "neither" — in a third behavioural state. Later experiments backed this up: no-pallium animals had deficits on working-memory tasks, xenocortical animals did not. Sergio's judgement is that function was preserved in the animals that received human cortical cells, and human cells very likely contributed some of it — but this is not perfect restoration, only evidence that these cells can integrate functionally and produce behavioural consequences.

7:11 A hypoxia experiment shows it is the human cells doing the work
The team used this system to model brain injury. Hypoxia is severe in humans and can cause lifelong disease, while mice tolerate low oxygen far better. After the three kinds of mice were exposed to low-oxygen conditions for several hours, the human cells were induced to mount a hypoxia response, while the mouse brain was relatively resilient. Two days later, on a motor task, wild-type mice and no-pallium mice were fine, but the xenocortical mice carrying human cells began to show defects in walking and gait coordination. Sergio thinks this shows it is very likely the human cells causing these defects, and that this would be a powerful system — not only for asking about mechanism but for testing therapies, to see whether there is benefit before going into clinical trials.

8:12 A very rare neuron type was grown
Aparna Bhaduri at the University of California studies human brain development and cancer. She thinks one highlight of the work is that a cell type differentiated from the human organoids looks like a very rare kind of neuron that has been hard to culture in vitro. Loss of this neuron type is a key factor in a particular dementia, so understanding them better could help future therapy development. But she also points out there is a long way to go: the cortex's layer structure and its different processing areas are not well preserved in this system, so it does not reach something more like a human brain; and the authors themselves note that the developmental stage the organoids reach is still mid-development — this is not a fully mature cortex.

9:12 This is not a human brain in a mouse's head
Asked whether these animals count as human-mouse chimeras, Aparna Bhaduri says plainly: this is not a human brain inside a mouse. There are three reasons — it is immature; the complexity of cell types is insufficient, some cell types are still missing, and the cell types present are not mature; and although there are some connections with the rodent, the degree and the way they are wired differ from the human brain. So on complexity, maturity and connectivity, she sees this as an organoid pushed forward in its development, not a human brain. Other researchers Nature spoke to agree: these are not fully formed functional human cortex.

10:13 Ethicists are not a stumbling block for scientists
Emily Jackson at the London School of Economics studies the regulation of stem-cell-related research, including brain organoids. She says the most striking thing about this paper, and about the work of Sergio Pasca's lab, is the team's focus on the importance of ethics and regulation. She thinks people sometimes mistakenly treat regulation as an obstacle to scientists, and that this is a genuine error: in her experience, scientists at the frontier of biotechnology very much want ethicists involved, very much want to know where the red lines are, so that they can proceed in the confidence that society approves. She also stresses that when you replace part of a rodent's brain with human brain cells, the key question is what harm this does to the animal — especially a new kind of harm that you would not easily notice, which must be taken very seriously.

17:19 Turning a paper into an agent you can talk to
James's team at Stanford proposes turning static papers into "knowledge agents" — think of them as a paper's virtual corresponding author. Their workflow is called paper to agent: a set of AI agents reads the paper through, works out how it was done, reproduces the original results, and then stores the knowledge in a server, acting as a translation layer between the human paper and any AI, so that models like ChatGPT and Claude become virtual co-authors you can ask anything about the paper — even run analyses with your own data. James stresses this differs from simply throwing the paper into a chatbot: the latter only reads, interprets and summarises results, does not know how the results and figures were generated, and cannot use the data and code, because it has no hands-on experience; a paper agent has that hands-on experience.

item.content:encoded:
In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.

This episode has medium information density, but the first half — a first-hand account of how evidence standards in medical AI went from chaos to discipline — is directly useful to anyone building medical AI products.

11:22 Fewer than 5% of AI papers in top journals hold up
Around 2019, every week brought new papers claiming "AI is as good as radiologists" or "AI beats radiologists at pneumonia detection," yet these conclusions contradicted each other. Xiao Liu and her collaborators did something no one was doing at the time: they took the rigor standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years and applied them to these AI papers, keeping only those with external validation, like-for-like comparisons, and meaningful control groups. The paper count was cut down dramatically — fewer than 5% truly met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. And within that small set, the best models only matched radiologists. This isn't bad news; it means there's too much noise in the published literature.

16:28 Reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did
CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, STARD, TRIPOD — these reporting guidelines are essentially checklists specifying which items a paper must report. They don't tell you how to do the research — they're not methodology guidelines, they're transparency guidelines. Whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. Their function is to put authors, journal editors, and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke bombs, no hiding behind vague details. Xiao Liu added a side effect: when authors know they must report a certain item, it can in turn push methodological rigor upward, though that's hard to measure.

18:33 Guidelines are produced by Delphi voting; items without consensus get cut
CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI weren't written by a few people behind closed doors; they went through a Delphi process: first a literature review and expert opinion generated a set of candidate items, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, ending with an in-person discussion. That in-person discussion is often the most valuable, because people learn from each other. Items that fail to reach consensus are excluded; only those that do are kept. Xiao Liu says doing this kind of consensus project well takes at least six months; she tried a compressed three-month version, but participants contribute their time for free, and to get high-quality feedback and multiple rounds of participation, you can't skimp on time or reach.

20:36 Whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines was fought over at the meeting
Andy Beam recalls that one question in the Delphi discussion was: should clinical trials include explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluations you did. He and Lauren Oakden-Rayner got up on the small stage and said "No, it shouldn't be done at all, and here's why." That debate was later commissioned into a paper by Lancet Digital Health editor Rupa, and it became one of Andy's most cited papers. Xiao Liu also clearly takes the "no" side in the lightning round: she thinks you should first ask why you want AI explainability, and keep asking until you reach the bottom — what you ultimately want is just beneficial effects.

26:43 Being a regulatory consultant without ever working in industry felt insincere
At the time, Xiao Liu was doing academic AI research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulators. She began to feel she had never stood on the regulated side, and that consulting was a bit insincere. So she joined Apple as a health scientist, mainly designing validation studies for wearable device algorithms, such as Apple Watch sensing algorithms, including a hypertension notification feature released this year. She says Apple has a well-oiled product shipping machine, which was exactly the experience she wanted. After more than a year, she returned to Birmingham to build a lab full-time, and then joined Microsoft AI's newly formed medical frontier LLM team.

32:49 Short term, computer scientists set direction; long term, clinicians gatekeep
Asked whether medical AI will be driven more by computer scientists or clinicians, Xiao Liu first asked what "driven" means, and after confirming it means "changed," gave her judgment: short term, computer scientists and engineers; long term, clinicians. The mechanism: the people who process data, choose metrics, and choose benchmarks determine which direction progress goes in the short term; but if the endpoint is truly being used on patients, clinicians will play the gatekeeper role at a later stage.

33:50 Doctors' work won't change much in five years, but should in ten
Xiao Liu thinks doctors' work won't look dramatically different within five years, but very likely will in ten years and beyond — and she hopes it will. The path she envisions: if medical intelligence and models keep advancing at the current pace, the medical profession no longer has to be about accumulating knowledge, or even about the kind of medical reasoning taught in medical school; the focus shifts to being a "companion to experience" — accompanying deteriorating health, sudden health events, daily wellbeing fluctuations, life-changing diagnoses, treatment failures and complications, and perhaps recovery, perhaps not. She thinks people will continuously need something deeply interpersonal on this journey: someone who can call on knowledge but doesn't necessarily carry it themselves, instead translating it into human language.

40:00 The most optimistic thing is dismantling old medical concepts; the most pessimistic is that we dare not
Xiao Liu says she is more optimistic than pessimistic. What excites her most is that aggregating all the knowledge in the medical world might reveal that our understanding of biomarkers, disease phenotype clustering, and existing medical knowledge frameworks is off. She gives her own PhD research on inflammatory eye diseases as an example: a bunch of diseases are loosely called "white dot syndromes" just because they produce white dots in the fundus, but they are likely driven by completely different mechanisms. She hopes one way new intelligence emerges is by dismantling these old concepts in medicine. The pessimistic side: this field is inherently cautious and may resist such dismantling out of unfamiliarity, sticking rigidly to the evaluation methods and guidelines of the past ten or twenty years during a period of new technological change, missing the chance for discovery.

item.title: He Treated Cancer With Bacterial Toxins and Was Dismissed by His Peers for Forty Years

item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he couldn't standardize the treatment or explain its mechanism, and radiation and regulation pushed it out; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around it.
item.content:encoded:
Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he couldn't standardize the treatment or explain its mechanism, and radiation and regulation pushed it out; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around it.

Medium information density: the first half is medical-history background, but the second half — on why the therapy was abandoned and how immunotherapy picked up the thread — is where the value is.

6:13 The death of an 18-year-old patient changed him
In 1890, Coley took on 17-year-old Bessie Dashiell, who had persistent pain after injuring her hand and was eventually diagnosed with periosteal sarcoma. Coley amputated below the elbow, but the tumor soon appeared elsewhere, and she died on January 23, 1891, at just 18 years old, only about 10 weeks after Coley first examined her. Coley was 28 at the time, in his first year as a surgeon. Amputation was the only treatment available and it had not worked, which drove him to comb through roughly 90 records of cancer surgery patients at New York Hospital from the previous 15 years in search of something better.

7:15 In one record, the tumor had vanished on its own
In the case files, Coley found a case of small round cell sarcoma of the neck in a patient of his colleague Dr. William T. Bull: four recurrences, and by the fifth operation the tumor had invaded deep structures and could not be removed. After surgery the patient accidentally developed erysipelas of the face and neck, which flared up again two weeks later. Within days of the first attack the tumor began to soften and shrank rapidly, and by the time the patient was discharged the tumor had disappeared completely. The hospital had no follow-up records, so Coley went door to door in the German immigrant community and found him: in the spring of 1891 he was still alive, with no local or systemic recurrence, seven years after the surgery.

9:21 He tried live bacteria first, then switched to toxins
On May 2, 1891, Coley began trying to induce erysipelas in a patient with inoperable sarcoma of the tonsil and neck. The tumor was so large the patient could not eat solid food and could only swallow small amounts of liquid. Coley exposed the patient to bacteria cultured in the lab, but for months could not induce erysipelas, until in October an injection of a culture a colleague had brought from Robert Koch's laboratory in Germany made the patient gravely ill — yet two weeks later the neck tumor was gone, the tonsil tumor had shrunk, and the patient lived in good health for eight years. By the end of 1892, after two early patients died of infection, Coley began working with bacteriologists to heat-kill the bacteria and filter out the toxins rather than use live bacteria directly.

15:34 The effect was real, but only in some patients
In his papers, Coley wrote that in his own experience, in slightly more than 10% of cases the regression process continued until the tumor was completely absorbed and the patient remained cured; in other cases the improvement was only temporary, and within weeks the tumor grew back and the patient died despite continued injections at higher doses; and in a very few cases, especially large, highly vascular tumors, particularly of the melanotic type, no clearly beneficial effect was ever observed. By 1909 he was recommending the treatment for all inoperable sarcomas (except melanotic ones), for osteosarcoma of the long bones where surgery meant sacrificing a limb, for primary sarcoma after surgery once the wound had healed as a preventive against recurrence, and for all carcinomas after surgery to reduce recurrence.

19:40 JAMA withheld judgment, then declared failure two months later
On May 31, 1894, Coley read his paper before the American Surgical Association. In October of that year, JAMA published an article comparing bacterial toxins to diphtheria antitoxin, saying the best method of use had not yet been determined, that it was still experimental, and calling for patience until experts delivered complete results. But only two months later, on December 15, 1894, JAMA published "The Failure of the Erysipelas Toxins," saying there was "no longer much question that the toxin injections as a cure for sarcoma and malignant growths have completely failed," and that although many surgeons had faithfully tried it over the previous six months, not a single fully verified recovery had been reported. Coley responded the following January, noting that he had used not only erysipelas toxins but also Bacillus prodigiosus, and arguing that the failure of a few doctors in a limited number of cases would not settle the scientific community's judgment of whether the method succeeded.

23:47 Forty years, a thousand patients, a hundred and fifty papers
Coley worked with these toxins for about 40 years, treating roughly 1,000 cancer patients and publishing about 150 papers. In 1909 he wrote that 52 cases of inoperable sarcoma had been successfully treated with a mixed toxin of erysipelas and Bacillus prodigiosus, of which 35 remained healthy for 3.25 to 16 years, 28 for 5 to 16 years, and 14 for 10 to 16 years. Although Park, Davis, and Company had been producing various preparations since 1899, the toxins never became the most common treatment for inoperable sarcoma. The reasons included: tense relations with his boss James Ewing, who opposed his research; the bone sarcoma registry refusing to include his cured patients, insisting they had been misdiagnosed; his insistence that all cancers had a microbial origin, even after that idea had been overturned; the difficulty of producing and standardizing the toxins; and the 1902 Biologics Control Act, which raised the regulatory cost.

26:54 Radiation took away his window
Coley's own method of use was also fairly loose: different patients received different doses by different methods for different lengths of time. Partly this was because he was trying to figure out what worked and how best to do it, but some treatment decisions were made almost on feel rather than data. He also noted that other doctors using his toxins treated patients for much longer than he did, conceding that his own shorter courses might explain some patients' recurrences. X-rays were discovered in 1895 and radium in 1898, and radiation quickly became the standard treatment for many inoperable cancers. Both discoveries came early in his writing about the therapy. In 1934, JAMA published a statement from its Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry, slightly more positive in wording than 40 years earlier, saying the mixed toxins of erysipelas and prodigiosus might sometimes play an important role in preventing or delaying malignant recurrence or metastasis, and might occasionally cure hopeless inoperable tumors. But by then Coley had already retired, and he died on April 16, 1936, at the age of 74.

29:00 His daughter spent her life building an institute for her father
After Coley's death, his daughter Helen Coley Nauts began organizing his papers and correspondence, intending to write a biography, and ended up delving deep into his work. She had no medical qualifications and no formal education beyond high school, but she carefully went through all of her father's publications, trying to work out what made the difference between success and failure. In 1953, she partnered with philanthropist Oliver R. Gray Sr. to found the Cancer Research Institute, with funding from sources including Nelson Rockefeller. She served as its director until her death in 2001. Her brother Bradley was also an advocate of their father's method and became chief of bone surgery at Memorial Hospital after their father retired. The Cancer Research Institute today has an award named after Coley, recognizing outstanding research in basic and tumor immunology.

item.title: Government Doesn't Just Waste Your Money, It Wastes an Hour of Your Week

item.description: Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants, and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.
item.content:encoded:
Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants, and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.

Medium information density, but the "time tax" framing itself is valuable: it reprices the administrative friction of the welfare state as a regressive levy. The confession in the back half about softening on UBI is worth hearing.

0:58 The IRS is legally barred from filing your taxes for you
Lowrey's core example: in Japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries send you a pre-filled return and you just correct errors. The US could absolutely do this — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, and their tax situations are fairly simple — but the IRS is not legally permitted to. This is not a technology problem, it's an institutional choice. She defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost the government shifts onto individuals as administrative labor, and unlike a monetary tax, it's different: you can earn more money, you can't earn more time.

1:02 The worst program is TANF, not the IRS
Lowrey names TANF (cash welfare) as the single worst program in government: nominally meant to address child poverty, it doesn't actually change the child poverty rate, its compliance burden is extremely onerous and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. She offers a rule — programs aimed at high-income Americans are far better experiences, safety-net programs are generally bad, and welfare is the worst. This yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political influence of its beneficiaries.

6:08 Pandemic fraud isn't something the time tax can prevent
Cowen raises a common objection: after deregulation in 2020, fraud exploded, so maybe the time tax is a necessary cost of fraud prevention. Lowrey rejects this outright: the fraud came mainly from criminal gangs and fake small businesses, and from the fact that the UI system itself runs on ancient COBOL infrastructure. Her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have zero incentive to upgrade UI systems when unemployment is low, so every recession replays the same conversation. The conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not.

11:19 Large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side
Lowrey points out that Medicare and Medicaid fraud is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics, and hospital systems defrauding the government. Individual fraud has a low ceiling, because the amount you can extract from the government is limited; to commit large-scale fraud, you have to process a lot of paperwork. So her policy ordering is: reduce administrative overhead in other programs, concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organizations and legitimate providers, rather than burdening the 99.9% who don't commit fraud. She adds a political-economy note: fraud narratives are often used to make programs seem illegitimate, so voters tolerate cuts.

13:25 50 hours per person per year, and highly unequal
Lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the American Time Use Survey: total bureaucratic time is about 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. She acknowledges this is an underestimate — ATUS can't capture multitasking (waiting on hold while cooking counts as one activity), and the time tax is scattered across categories without being aggregated. Who pays the most? People entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. The rich can "skip" it with subordinates and accountants, but there's one exception: renovating a house in San Francisco requires waiting 500 days and going through multiple rounds of public review no matter how rich you are.

22:57 AI can fill out forms, but it can't fill a urine test
Cowen asks whether AI agents could handle all this within five years. Lowrey says probably, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most burdensome programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is unknown; second, many burdens aren't paperwork at all — they're mandatory interviews, urine screenings, hard-to-collect data. She gives SNAP as an example: benefits are calculated by household, but the government has no stable definition of "household," and you have to explain how you split staple food costs with co-residents — a question AI would struggle to answer for you. She mentions she was originally skeptical, but a civic technologist who has worked in this field for years firmly believes AI will help a great deal.

31:18 Disability insurance is already hard enough to apply for
Cowen presses with data: from 1990 to 2014, the number of people on disability insurance roughly quadrupled while workplace deaths kept falling — shouldn't the threshold be raised? Lowrey doesn't accept the inference. She offers two alternative explanations: population aging and rising obesity-related chronic illness. Then she gives a counterpoint: 5% of applicants must submit over 1,000 pages of medical material; 11,000 Americans die each year while waiting for a disability determination. She admits she worries about both sides — both about paying people who don't need it and about denying people who truly do — so she doesn't think this is the moment to add more paperwork.

38:28 Her UBI stance has been shaken by the research
Lowrey's previous book, Give People Money, was pro-UBI; this time she says explicitly that the research findings are "sobering," and she has updated her priors: the ancillary benefits she expected cash to deliver haven't materialized. But her defense is that the point of giving people money is to give people money to buy things, and that rationale still holds; life improvements falling short of expectations is not a reason to oppose the policy. On AI and UBI, she admits she was extremely dismissive back then of the claim that "AI will force UBI," and she won't go that far now, but if GDP and productivity surge while unemployment also rises, that would be very strange, and we'd have to start considering UBI-type policies.

item.title: After 25 Million Users at Tome, He Tore It Down to Build a CRM
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-a16z-tome-做到-2500-万用户后-他推倒重来去做-crm/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-a16z-tome-做到-2500-万用户后-他推倒重来去做-crm/
item.description: Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he judged that the CRM battle isn't about making salespeople do more work, but about whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.
item.content:encoded:
Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he judged that the CRM battle isn't about making salespeople do more work, but about whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.

The first half is a rare post-mortem on deliberately shutting down a growing product; the second half is dense with operational detail on pricing, expansion and org design.

3:01 They killed a hit not because of the data, but because they didn't like it
Tome launched around the same time as ChatGPT and reached 2 million monthly users, so many that inference capacity ran short and people had to queue. But Keith says what really made them stop wasn't a metric — it was that "none of us liked the product." Concretely: they couldn't see a path where a discerning, high-quality presentation maker would treat Tome as indispensable, nor one where investment banking or consulting people would use it to write memos. Their conclusion was that what the models lacked at the time wasn't general reasoning ability but context about who the presenter is, who the audience is, and what relationship holds between them — and that gap wasn't something a stronger model would close.

6:04 Follow the heat first, then discover the real problem is data
The Tome team dug through its own user base and found B2B users clustered in sales and marketing, so they ran free pilots with 12 large companies. The original idea was to help sales build new-business decks and proposals, but customers started asking: can you also do research, help us qualify leads, help us understand which companies are worth expanding into. They followed that pull, asking customers to open up access to CRM, call recordings and data warehouses, and found the hardest part wasn't doing that work — it was that the data in these systems contradicted itself. The reality in call recordings and the reality in the CRM often didn't line up. Keith says reorganizing that data started to look like the most important work, so they concluded: if you could reorganize a company's reality into something both machines and people could understand, that was more worth doing than the original path.

8:11 Nobody wants your four-month-old CRM, so pay them to use it
They started with a go-to-market assistant that AEs used every day but that they couldn't charge for — because the data wasn't theirs, and ten other companies were chasing the same thing. So they cut headcount, rethought the CRM from scratch, worked in stealth for four months, and then discovered nobody wanted a four-month-old CRM. The only asset left was a huge office lease they couldn't get out of, so they posted on X and LinkedIn: use our CRM and we'll let you sit in our office for free. That's "negative pricing." The 10 startups they brought in were there every day, complaining about slowness and missing features, but giving feedback in Slack every two hours. Keith says this was the exact opposite of Tome: a barely working product that users were inside every day and cared enough about to give hourly feedback.

11:21 The core of a CRM is relationships, not fields
Three of Lightfield's five founders came from Facebook. Their plain judgment was that the most important thing in a CRM is modeling relationships, so they borrowed directly from the Facebook timeline and first built an activity log — when you first made contact, what you said, what they replied, which meetings happened, which documents went back and forth, and eventually what the other party did inside your product and how they paid. All the traditional CRM field updates and stage progressions are triggered from that log, but underneath there is always a canonical relationship log. They also tried going fully unstructured and found queries too slow — a needle-in-a-haystack problem — and landed on semi-structured: stuff a large amount of unstructured data into the activity log and let the system infer causality from the log.

15:26 Get the data model wrong and sales will never go back and fix it
They interviewed a lot of CRM consultants, asking what they actually do for clients, and found the highest-consequence thing is the data model: set your stages and fields wrong and you can't send salespeople back in time to fill in the data — it's over. So Lightfield chose to be "schema-less": connect email, drop in a call recording, hook up the data warehouse, and the system assembles the relationship in real time; fields come later. Change your mind and it traverses the activity log and backfills. Alex Rampell summed this up as "intelligence is greater than schema," and contrasted it with the old era: back then, to save space, every column in a table had to have a predefined varchar length, like name varchar 25 — now they don't even want a schema.

17:28 Someone used it to find a cutting-edge treatment for an Alzheimer's patient
Because it supported fully arbitrary schemas, custom objects and custom relationships from the start, Lightfield attracted a set of customers with very strange business models. Keith's example is Power: on one side it serves pharma companies, helping them find clinical trial subjects; on the other it's a marketplace aggregating patients with hard-to-diagnose conditions and searching for cutting-edge treatments. They modeled both the B2C and B2B sides in Lightfield, wrote automations to scrape the FDA and clinicaltrials.gov, built a world model of "every ongoing clinical trial in the world," and then matched patients to pharma companies. The result: Lightfield actually helped an Alzheimer's patient find a cutting-edge treatment within days.

23:37 Win the founders and engineers first, then wait for the sales VP to come around
Alex points out something often overlooked: the sales VP a greenfield company hires was trained by Salesforce and will say flat out, "I don't use that." Lightfield's design principle is to win first the founders, engineering leads and product leads — the people willing to use frontier technology to understand customers — while making every sales-led option freely available to anyone in the company. That both helps the company understand what engineering, support and finance are doing and creates real intra-company network effects that make replacement harder. By the time that senior sales VP arrives and finds engineering, finance and support all using it for customer understanding and account scoring, the company pushes him to try it — and that's when they get their opening.

32:00 Pure seat-based and pure consumption pricing both crashed
They first tried pure seat-based pricing. Customers accepted it fine, but top users consumed 10,000 times what the tail did, which wasn't sustainable long term. Then they tried pure consumption pricing, turning everything into credits — and within three weeks nobody touched any feature. Keith says those were the company's worst three weeks: a pile of signups and no usage. Finally they split it into four kinds of work: everyday CRM work (logging meetings, filling fields, updating tasks) goes into a platform fee or seat fee, because customers don't want to budget annually for "the margin of error on core CRM"; pipeline generation is charged on consumption, because there's alpha there that turns into revenue; workflow automation is charged separately — say someone requests a demo on your website and Lightfield decides this one is for Henry at the deep tech company and that one is for Matt at the health tech company; and finally intelligence and prediction, which Keith considers Lightfield's most untapped part, where customers will pay for the alpha.

item.title: Bad teeth are the number one reason kids go to A&E? The number got misread
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-moreorless-儿童看急诊第一原因是牙-数字被念错了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-moreorless-儿童看急诊第一原因是牙-数字被念错了/
item.description: A British MP said teeth are the top reason children end up in A&E. The actual figure refers to 5-to-18-year-olds hospitalised for tooth decay — not the same thing, and the decay rate is actually drifting down.
item.content:encoded:
A British MP said teeth are the top reason children end up in A&E. The actual figure refers to 5-to-18-year-olds hospitalised for tooth decay — not the same thing, and the decay rate is actually drifting down.

Four fact-checks strung into one episode: fast pace, medium information density. The teeth and medicines segments have the most solid numbers; the NEET and P-Doom segments work better as thinking exercises.

1:01 Teeth are the top reason for A&E visits — that claim is wrong
Leila Moran, a Liberal Democrat MP and chair of the Health and Social Care Committee, said on Radio 4's The World at One that the number one reason children go to A&E is teeth. Chris Venatza, a consultant in paediatric dentistry at Newcastle University, flatly rejected it: she very likely conflated two sets of numbers. What actually ranks first is "hospital admission for tooth decay treatment" — the leading cause of hospital admission for children aged 5 to 18. A&E visits, by contrast, have all sorts of causes, and there is simply no data showing whether dentistry ranks high or low among them. Moran's office later confirmed Chris was right, and that she had meant the hospital admission figure, not the A&E figure.

3:09 Lots of hospital tooth extractions, because the rules changed in 2001
When children are hospitalised for teeth, it is usually not for a filling but for an extraction. Extractions are harder for a child to endure, so children who cannot cooperate for an extraction in a dental clinic may need general anaesthetic. There is an institutional turning point here: in 2001 the rules changed, and ordinary dental practices were no longer allowed to administer general anaesthetic — anyone needing it had to go to hospital. So a large share of the hospital admission numbers are general-anaesthetic extractions. This explains why "hospital admission" and "A&E" are two entirely different measures: one is a surgical arrangement pushed into hospitals by the rules, the other is an unplanned visit.

4:10 The admission rate is actually falling, not a crisis
Chris gives the admission rate per 100,000 population: about 320 in 2015, down to 270 before the pandemic, and 250 now. Host Tim Harford's reaction was that this doesn't look like a crisis, and the trend is even rather encouraging. Chris concedes that falling before the pandemic is a good thing, but stresses that even so, a large number of children are still having general anaesthetic and having dental treatment in hospital, which in itself is not good. He adds one more thing: over the past decade, dental causes have consistently been the number one reason for hospital admission, unchanged for ten years — so the "number one" position is stable, but the absolute level is heading down.

5:10 To see the decay rate, look at school surveys, not admissions
Chris says there is a better dataset for understanding the true state of children's tooth decay: the government sends dentists into schools to examine five-year-olds. The latest survey found 22% of five-year-olds already have decay reaching the dentine layer — close to a quarter. A quarter of the population having a disease that needs treatment, he says, is not a good state of affairs. Over time: about 30.9% in 2008, down to 23% by 2017-2018, then a plateau, with the latest survey slightly down again from the 2022 one. Longer-term data comes from a survey run once a decade since 1973: 72% of five-year-olds had decay in 1973, down to 43% in 2003 — roughly halved.

8:15 25% of UK medicines come from Israel — off by two orders of magnitude
US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said on the Today programme that 25% of the medicines Britain uses come from Israel. Lizzie McNeill checked the latest ONS import data: in 2025 the UK imported £10 million of medicines from Israel, against total UK medicine imports of about £28 billion — Israel accounts for just 0.04%, one twenty-fifth of 1%, not 25%. She also rules out several possibilities: active pharmaceutical ingredients come mainly from India and China, and the more upstream raw materials mainly from China; medicines supplied by Israeli companies (the largest being Teva) are mostly not made in Israel but in European plants in Hungary, Croatia and elsewhere. Teva estimates it supplies one in eight generic medicine packs in the UK, equivalent to one ninth of all prescriptions, but the other Israeli companies are all too small to push the total to 25%.

13:29 Blame Gove for rising NEETs, and Wales dismantles the case
Education Secretary Lucy Powell wrote in The Times that a million young people have been left behind by the education system Michael Gove led. Daisy Christodoulou rebuts with a natural experiment: Wales and Scotland took the opposite path to Gove's reforms. Wales's NEET rate for 16-to-24-year-olds rose from 14% in 2019 to 17% in 2025, while England's rose from 11% to 13% over the same period — similar levels, similar trend, with Wales rising slightly more. If Gove is responsible for England's rise, then Wales must be responsible for Wales's rise, yet the two places had completely opposite policies. She says the NEET rate sits on top of economic structure, minimum wage, tax, regulation and far too many other factors — not just education.

17:51 The teen mental health decline is not unique to England
Against the criticism that Gove's reforms increased academic pressure and damaged mental health, Daisy turns to the WHO's Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey, which reports England, Scotland and Wales separately. It shows average life satisfaction among teenagers fell in all three places this century (2000 to 2022), but it also fell across Western Europe and many other regions, so it is not specific to England. Then the share of 15-year-olds who "like school a lot": about 10% in England, about 9% in Scotland, about 7.5% in Wales — all low, but basically the same across the three. The share of 15-year-olds overwhelmed by academic pressure is high in all three, with no big difference.

19:59 P-Doom is a subjective probability, and nobody can produce a model
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, warning that Anthropic and OpenAI are irresponsible on AI safety. Anthropic's Evan Hubinger responded on X: he personally thinks the probability that AI kills all of humanity within the next decade is greater than 10%. Alexander Mark Koch, an assistant professor of global risk and resilience at Cambridge, explains that P-Doom is shorthand for "the probability that AI causes human extinction", and is almost always one individual's subjective probability estimate. He says the issue is extraordinarily complex: it involves regulatory capacity, system resilience, where large-model capabilities are heading, autonomous weapons and biotech tools, whether AI can self-improve into an exponential loop, funding, rules, what China will do, and disaster scenarios ranging from science fiction to "a rogue state using a large model to learn to build bioweapons".

item.title: Sequoia's Former Boss on Reading People: What Happens Before 14 Sets Your Core
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
