Both Kimi and ZAI announced models first and uploaded weights to Hugging Face almost exactly three weeks later. He isn't sure whether this is an internal regulatory process — every AI lab in China has to communicate with the government and register releases — but finds the coincidence too strange. Nathan adds: this industry has never had a tradition of giving release partners a lot of extra time, it's usually "here's the model, hot potato, good luck," so if you really can get weights a few weeks early, that itself is a signal.

item.title: US Treasury Yields Near 5%: Why the AI Narrative Hasn't Broken Yet
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-cna29e88-美债利率逼近5-ai叙事为何还不破/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-cna29e88-美债利率逼近5-ai叙事为何还不破/
item.description: US money is getting more expensive, yet AI is still inflating while every other sector deflates. This contradiction either gets resolved by AI delivering a real breakthrough that pulls rates down, or by AI being falsified — but nobody dares slow down first.
item.content:encoded:
US money is getting more expensive, yet AI is still inflating while every other sector deflates. This contradiction either gets resolved by AI delivering a real breakthrough that pulls rates down, or by AI being falsified — but nobody dares slow down first.

Two institutional investors review Q3 global markets, focusing on the three-layer logic behind rising US Treasury yields and the AI prisoner's dilemma. The judgment leans cautious — suited to anyone trying to understand the relationship between the cost of capital and the AI narrative.

3:00 Q3 markets: the exhaustion comes from having no direction
In Q3 the S&P rose 2.1%, the Nasdaq was roughly flat, Japan and Korea fell 8-something and 18.5 respectively, the CSI 300 dropped 9.4, ChiNext fell 23 points, and the Hang Seng rose 8 points though Hang Seng Tech remained very weak. Commodities were the bright spot: WTI and Brent both rose 40 points over the quarter, and gold rose 8.5. But the host says his own feeling is ‘a strong sense of exhaustion’ — unlike the first half, when hearing a narrative and watching the market move still made you wonder what opportunity there was, whether to buy or sell, how to allocate. Now it's ‘tired, forget it.’ Ricky's summary: the first half was making money with your heart in your throat; this quarter was adjusting in total exhaustion.

17:13 Three forces driving US Treasury yields higher
A Clock Tower research note attributes the rise in US long-end yields to three forces: first, energy prices rising as the Middle East stalemate drags on and becomes long-term; second, resilient US nominal growth — Q2 real GDP growth of about 1.5 plus core PCE inflation of 3.4 adds up to 5% nominal growth, comparable to the late 1990s, when the combined level of US Treasury yields was around 5%; third, rapid expansion of corporate bond issuance as AI infrastructure buildout continues, and all of this against a backdrop of already-high US fiscal deficits. The remedies correspond to Middle East de-escalation, tighter macro policy, and a substantive slowdown in the AI investment cycle — but the latter two contradict each other.

21:17 Bond yields are credit pricing, not a buy-sell mismatch
Ricky explains it by going up a dimension: a bond yield is fundamentally the cost of funds generated on the basis of credit. After the Soviet failure in the late 1980s and early 1990s, the US entered a long period of low rates, because it was the most powerful country in the world and its borrowing cost should be the lowest in the world. Since 2018 the US has entered the mid-to-late phase of its national fortune cycle, facing more and more doubt, its credit downgraded, and so its borrowing cost must rise. In the two-dimensional world you see fewer buyers of Treasuries and more redeemers; in the three-dimensional world you see a decline in national power driving up borrowing costs. The US decision at the three-dimensional level is to keep pushing on AI, mobilising the whole country for AI buildout while also pushing manufacturing reshoring — which sets private capital and state capital competing for money, and everyone's borrowing cost rises.

26:20 Will AI infrastructure repeat the ROA trap of the great infrastructure buildout
Ricky compares US AI infrastructure to China's great infrastructure buildout starting in 2008: an economic entity dominated by CAPEX will inevitably see ROA decline — more and more assets, no breakthrough in production technology, so the return per unit of asset falls. When ROA drops below the borrowing cost, an asset crisis follows. The biggest worry now is that AI infrastructure will end up with ROA unable to cover the borrowing cost, while the borrowing cost is rising and the improvement in ROA is not yet obvious. David Weng adds: what's different this time is that deficits weren't this high before — past cycles didn't casually run into trillions the way they do now, and the current magnitude has gone beyond the range of human comprehension.

41:29 The prisoner's dilemma behind the calls to slow AI down
This week Dario wrote "We must pace the frontier," Musk reposted it saying he agreed, and Sam Altman also said in an interview that things should slow down, even saying OpenAI isn't in a hurry to IPO this year. A Reuters article on September 9 was titled "Researchers want AI to slow down, but labs can't afford to." Ricky sees it in three layers: first, right and wrong in the two-dimensional world cannot be overturned in the three-dimensional world — Asimov's Three Laws saw it a hundred years ago, and you can't stop a disaster before it happens; second, a unified alliance of three or more players is unachievable — the prisoner's dilemma ends with everyone choosing the worst outcome, and it needs an external force, which is government, but government only abandons its own problems once great-power competition produces enough damage and disaster; third, the funding side cannot tolerate such a long verification period — if within a year large models haven't proven they have a sufficient application and commercial environment, a lot of money will see runs and even broken funding chains, at a magnitude that would certainly be countless times that of the 2008 subprime crisis.

51:38 Large-model revenue of 150 billion against 200 billion of investment
Ricky does the math: across large models, revenue is 150 billion and investment is 200 billion. Split into frontier models and open-source models: frontier models bring in about 120 billion dollars of revenue on 100 billion of investment; open-source models take 100 billion of investment for 300 billion... no — 30 billion of revenue. Frontier model revenue alone is just that, and open-source models are still a long way from actually generating revenue to cover investment — not even profit covering investment. So whether these companies will still post big profit gains next year is under heavy pressure. More critical is the second layer: even if corporate earnings still rise by a small double-digit percentage next year, will the capital market accept it? Because the second derivative is actually heading down, and valuations are set on the second derivative, not on earnings growth. If you can't count white-collar replacement, you can't make the math work — and then it's definitely expensive.

1:00:40 Midterms: the probability Trump loses the House is very high
From BCA's research: over more than a century of US history, every midterm where performance on livelihood issues and inflation was poor, the probability of losing the House and Senate was almost 100%. The path laid out on the show early this year was that by June, if the US-Iran issue were resolved, energy costs brought under control, and Trump added some fiscal policy support, there was hope of holding the Senate. But neither of those has happened, so judging by the polls the probability Trump loses the House is very high — many swing states and minorities like Hispanics, once Trump supporters, are starting to switch to the Democrats. The probability Trump holds the Senate should be high. If he only holds one chamber of Congress, he becomes a lame duck.

1:25:03 A-share rally in Q4, but don't play too far to the left
Ricky thinks A-shares can still look forward to a rally in Q4, but it shouldn't be played too far to the left; watch mainly the volume of funds — if there's a short-term amplification in fund flows, it's worth participating. After that participation, switch to full defence and wait for the next, larger-magnitude breakout point, such as something clear on white-collar replacement, or clearer investment next year in the Huawei supply chain and the DeepSeek supply chain. If this rebound comes, it will certainly be led by tech, because many sectors have been tried without effect, and only tech can drive the market up. In Q3 most fund managers did no work and were busy writing self-criticism; in Q4 they'll have to work no matter what. David Weng is more conservative: still put cash first, second dividend low-volatility, third a narrower slice of tech such as the STAR 50, with a position of maybe two or three points.

item.title: The AI Slowdown Debate: Dario's Three-Step Plan, and Both Sam and Elon Nodded
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-tbpn-ai-减速之争-dario-的三步计划-sam-和-elon-都点了头/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-tbpn-ai-减速之争-dario-的三步计划-sam-和-elon-都点了头/
item.description: Dario published a piece Saturday morning calling to "pace the frontier," and Sam and Elon both endorsed it the same day; but the only genuinely new fact is that OpenAI and Anthropic will embed third-party evaluators — and that step may require an antitrust exemption first.
item.content:encoded:
Dario published a piece Saturday morning calling to "pace the frontier," and Sam and Elon both endorsed it the same day; but the only genuinely new fact is that OpenAI and Anthropic will embed third-party evaluators — and that step may require an antitrust exemption first.

Medium information density, but it lays out the 48-hour weekend AI policy timeline, Dario's three-step plan and the objections from all sides in one pass — suited to anyone who hasn't kept up with this round of discussion.

3:30 Pace the frontier is not a new phrase — the line was laid in late July
The starting point of this discussion is not Dario's Saturday piece. On July 28, employees and leaders at OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind, Meta and other organisations signed an open letter on "pacing the frontier"; the same day Sam Altman said publicly that "we may have to slow down AI development"; two days later OpenAI told Axios that the letter's wording was shaped with OpenAI's involvement and that Altman had discussed pacing with White House officials. On August 18 OpenAI published a document on the pace of model development in the era of cyber-critical capabilities, saying it had indeed slowed scaling and paused one large RL training run — that was the two-week training pause. On August 31 an official Anthropic post explicitly discussed pacing the frontier and called for a coordination mechanism. On Saturday morning, September 12, Dario's piece turned this into a public campaign.

5:30 Dario's third step is the one that will actually blow up
Dario's three-step plan: one, let independent third-party evaluators into AI companies to verify safety practices — he named METER, which sparked the argument over whether METER is actually independent: METER has employees who worked at OpenAI and Anthropic, and people at Anthropic have been at METER, so it is a revolving door. Two, frontier labs and democratic governments establish AI safety standards with government help — the controversy here is whether labs need government approval. Three, the US and democracies should try to coordinate with authoritarian governments, meaning US-China coordination on AI pacing. The show points out the difficulty of step three: China still wants to catch up, and if both sides have exactly the same capabilities, is that the optimal equilibrium? If you always want to stay ahead, it is hard to negotiate with the other side to "keep only half the nuclear weapons we have."

8:00 Step two may require exempting the Sherman Antitrust Act first
Dario's step two asks frontier labs to coordinate safety standards with government help, and the show points out a hard legal problem here: the Sherman Antitrust Act has very clear rules about companies acting in concert. The analogy is that if American Airlines, Delta and United all said "for safety we should cut flights," the likely result would be less capacity, higher fares, higher profits and consumers harmed — which is exactly where the Sherman Act came from. So even if Demis, Dario, Sam and Elon all agree, actual federal regulatory rules would need to be adjusted or exempted. The show thinks this is precisely why Dario specifically calls for this step: it is easy to loosely agree in a blog post, but forming anything formal requires government approval.

10:00 David Sachs's six straight "stop pretending"s
David Sachs posted on X, first conceding "by any reasonable metric — market share, revenue growth, model capability — you are the frontier," noting that OpenAI and Anthropic have a duopoly on frontier intelligence, and claiming the lead is widening because of recursive self-improvement. Then he fired off six "stop pretending"s: stop pretending you need anyone's permission; stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel; stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that sits above product liability; stop pretending METER is independent when it is intertwined with Anthropic's investors and employees; stop pretending you need the same evaluators to govern competitors who are not at the frontier at all. The show also points out the regulatory capture angle: if safety rules become extremely onerous, a small team like Instinct that does not train frontier models would have to spend a year negotiating with third-party evaluators, embedding a crowd of people, and going through government review — and could never ship a hit consumer product.

14:30 Trump says the only guardrail AI needs is a high-IQ president
Trump was active over the weekend. He said the only control and guardrail AI needs is a strong, smart, high-IQ president, and that America has plenty of that. He also said this administration has already stopped AI people from doing bad things or things that could be bad, naming Dario, who now pretends to be a perfect little angel. He called it a sick conspiracy against AI and data centers, said the only one happy about it is China, and that whoever wins AI wins. Forty minutes later he posted again: when in business history has a leader of an industry called for regulation that, if strongly enforced, would push them into bankruptcy? He called AI taking over the world and destroying humanity a hoax, no different from Russia-gate, Ukraine-gate and the two impeachment hoaxes. He also mentioned that Xi Jinping had just announced China will put no obstacles on AI or its future, and that Google is building a big plant in Finland because US approvals are too hard.

18:30 Gavin Baker: the only new fact is third-party evaluators
Gavin Baker's weekend summary said that in 24 hours proposals were flying everywhere, and the TLDR is the only substantive new fact: OpenAI and Anthropic will embed third-party evaluators from unknown organisations, with Dario offering METER as one possibility. He thinks third-party evaluation is smart because model outputs have no Section 230-style liability shield, and showing a duty of care in future litigation matters — without Section 230, several internet companies might already be bankrupt. He judges the investment impact of this single new fact to be minimal. He also summarised Dario's proposal as: embed third-party evaluators, establish a national regulatory regime for models above some capability threshold, a broad international regulatory agreement among democracies, stricter compute distillation restrictions on China, and a different international regulatory regime that includes China.

20:30 Pacing could compress the frontier labs' own margins
The show offers a counterintuitive argument: if pacing actually happens, it could compress margins, because others catch up and the market becomes more oligopolistic. Right now OpenAI and Anthropic are a duopoly at the frontier, but if the current pace holds, MSL, DeepMind and Grok will all catch up to the same level, and in the end there will be four, five, six or seven genuinely capable competitors. Meanwhile Karazian said August AI spending fell slightly, mainly because of price cuts rather than people using it less — OpenAI is discounting, Fable's adoption is weak, and everyone is asking "are we sure we want to use a million-dollar model to check the weather." The show argues the pricing pressure on frontier labs comes not from Chinese open-source models but from the duopoly dynamic itself: enterprises are willing to do business with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or something running on AWS or Azure because it is mature, has SLAs and guaranteed uptime, whereas downloading DeepSeek weights and running it yourself is something many people do not want to deal with.

23:30 Nobody gives them credit for their PBC structure
Sam said in a Fortune interview that if this is bad for our business, we have told investors at every step for ten years that this is more like a non-profit, and there are many ways it is not purely aligned with shareholder interests like other companies — a PBC, a public benefit corporation. The show thinks both Sam and Dario are confident they can tell investors: we are doing something that will slow revenue growth, compress margins and even lower the company's market value, but we think it is right, and you cannot do anything about it because you invested in a PBC. But nobody really gives them credit for it; everyone sees it as a cynical move to get them to a ten-trillion-dollar market cap. The show sums it up with the bell curve meme: the low end is "slowing down is bad for business," the middle is "slowing down is actually four-dimensional chess and good for business," but the show itself says "I don't really buy it, though a lot of people online are saying it."

item.title: Jensen Huang: The AI Doom Narrative Is Made Up, and Superintelligence Is Already Here
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-allin-黄仁勋-ai-末日论是编出来的-超级智能已经到了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-allin-黄仁勋-ai-末日论是编出来的-超级智能已经到了/
item.description: Jensen Huang calls the frontier labs' extinction predictions "made up" and irresponsible, and says superintelligence is not future tense — in narrow domains like autonomous driving and protein synthesis, it already outperforms humans.
item.content:encoded:
Jensen Huang calls the frontier labs' extinction predictions "made up" and irresponsible, and says superintelligence is not future tense — in narrow domains like autonomous driving and protein synthesis, it already outperforms humans.

Huang's own full account of the doom narrative, open source, capital allocation and RSI, plus Trump calling in mid-episode. High information density, but the back half is the point.

4:05 The doom predictions should be settled line by line
Huang does not rebut AI risk in generalities; he lays out specific predictions from the past few years and audits them one by one: someone predicted radiologists would be fully replaced by AI within five years, and the result is that the world needs more radiologists, while AI did take over reading the scans; someone predicted 90% of code would be AI-generated within six to twelve months, wrong; someone predicted 50% of entry-level jobs would disappear within six to nine months, also wrong. His conclusion is that these predictions are "not based in science," and that the people making them should be held to account. The strength of this argument is not the position but that he drags the debate from "are you afraid" back to "were you right last time."

10:09 Danger can only come from the few with the most compute
Huang draws a compute-based boundary for regulation: every incident that has actually gone wrong so far has come from frontier labs, and the reason is not that they are less moral but that they have the most compute and are solving the most frontier problems. A high schooler cannot cause trouble because there is not enough compute; a startup will not be the source of risk either, for the same reason. So regulation should watch these few, and what these few should do is root-cause analysis in the engineering sense — when something goes wrong, find out what happened, what could have been done, and what technology and process to institutionalise. He adds one judgment: if these labs finish their analysis and say "we don't know what happened, we don't know how to control it, please help us, society," that is when other engineers should be let in to look.

13:10 RSI is an engineering process, not a runaway spiral
Confronted with news that Chinese labs are investing in recursive self-improvement, Huang breaks it into a concrete set of techniques: in-context learning, skills, reflection, reinforcement learning, synthetic data generation, plus methods like LoRA that improve a model without changing the base weights, and finally retraining the base on the accumulated experience. His key claim is that the control step cannot be skipped — you can RSI inside the company all day, but before a product ships it must be evaluated, must be tested, must be confirmed to have no regressions. So RSI does not lead to loss of control; rather, as labs shift from research to engineering and control tools get stronger, it gets boxed inside the company, and good products ship as usual.

17:13 Open models are the default for startups
Huang gives a set of numbers: in the last six months, $400 billion of venture money went into AI-native companies, and 80% of them use open models. His inference is that without open models these companies could not build what they want to build at all, because their dreams are not the frontier labs' dreams. He compares closed models to bottled water — water is free, use the right water in the right place — and both are needed. As for whether open models come from China or the US, his answer is that once you download it, it is yours: Linux and Kubernetes have been touched heavily by Chinese people, and you fork, improve and make it your own. From this he redefines the AI race as "who is best at using the technology," not who invented it first.

29:22 The doom story's anchor moved from national security to safety
Huang notices the narrative has swapped its fulcrum: it was first anchored in national security, that argument was thoroughly demolished recently, so now it is anchored in safety. He does not dismiss the safety issue because of this; instead he offers a concrete plan — labs themselves must be controllable and have good testing, third-party evaluators must exist, and there must be several of them, for the same reason as financial audits: an auditor need not understand the business better than the company, only ask the right questions; and multiple evaluators coexisting prevents any one of them from being steered by a single institution. The value of this passage is that it turns "should there be regulation" into "what should regulation look like."

35:27 Nvidia's strategy is to go up until it is enough
Asked why it went from chips all the way to Hugging Face, autonomous driving and biological models, Huang gives the principle: "go up until it is enough, go down as low as possible." His examples: without Nvidia doing cuDNN, the various frameworks would not exist; without Megatron Core, large-scale training would not happen. So Nvidia builds the necessary technology first, then lets a thousand flowers bloom. He admits he is "strangely non-competitive" and is happy to see five hyperscalers coexist. He also explains why NeoClouds have a place: hyperscalers plan once a year, and the market is too volatile, so they almost always plan wrong; regional clouds are more agile, know the local area better, and see land, power and buildings more clearly than people sitting in Seattle or Palo Alto.

40:30 It builds open models because customers need them, not to disrupt anyone
Huang explains that Nvidia's logic for doing open models is demand-driven: Alpamo is the world's first autonomous driving that thinks, relying on reasoning rather than billions of hours of road-test data, because many car, truck and freight companies are not big enough to build the whole stack themselves — Nvidia builds it and they do the last-mile adaptation. Biological models are the same — ESM2, ESMFold, OpenFold, AlphaFold 2, and Proteina Complexa for next-generation protein synthesis all exist because customers like Lilly and Merck need them and cannot yet do it themselves. His words: "We don't wake up thinking about disrupting someone, we wake up thinking about helping everyone."

44:31 Superintelligence has already happened, just in narrow domains
At the end of the episode Huang gives the most radical and most easily misread judgment of the hour: he does not think superintelligence is future tense. His way of defining it is by narrow domain — my autonomous driving does not need to make an omelette, it only needs to drive, and it drives better than a person, with an accident rate one tenth of a human's; synthesising proteins and doing virtual protein screening are domains that already exceed humans too. So his conclusion is that AGI has arrived, superintelligence is the next waypoint, but superintelligence already exists in narrow domains. This claim is the other end of the same argument as "AI will destroy humanity": he concedes neither loss of control nor that the capability is not yet here.

item.title: Nvidia's Flagship GPU Memory Regresses for the First Time: Why 4-HI HBM Wins
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-semianalysiswe-英伟达旗舰-gpu-内存首次倒退-4-hi-hbm-为什么赢/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-semianalysiswe-英伟达旗舰-gpu-内存首次倒退-4-hi-hbm-为什么赢/
item.description: Rubin Ultra's HBM was cut from a promised 1TB to 192GB, less than the 288GB shipping today. This isn't a technical step backward, it's capacity rationing under a DRAM shortage: 4-HI stacks yield better and can extract more than twice as many HBM cubes.
item.content:encoded:
Rubin Ultra's HBM was cut from a promised 1TB to 192GB, less than the 288GB shipping today. This isn't a technical step backward, it's capacity rationing under a DRAM shortage: 4-HI stacks yield better and can extract more than twice as many HBM cubes.

An episode that thoroughly explains the HBM height debate: from yields and bandwidth/capacity pricing to why model parameters are no longer exploding. High information density, and the second half's reasoning is worth more than the opening.

2:04 Rubin Ultra was cut from 1TB to 192GB
At GTC last year, when Nvidia previewed Rubin Ultra, it said 1TB of HBM per package: 4 compute dies, 16 HBM4E stacks, 32 gigabit (4GB) per die, 16-HI stacks. A year and a half later, the actual configuration is 192GB of HBM4: only 2 compute dies, 3GB per die of HBM4, 8-HI stacks. That's lower than the 288GB of Blackwell Ultra and vanilla Rubin, the first time in Nvidia's flagship GPU history that a next generation has less capacity than the previous one.

4:11 The spec cut was forced by DRAM supply
The motive is mainly supply. DRAM wafer capacity has barely increased, while accelerator shipments are rising, and HBM demand rises with them. Suppliers and customers like Nvidia, Google and Broadcom did the math: the logic capacity locked in at TSMC is fixed, and if that HBM is made into 12-HI cubes, there aren't enough cubes to match all the logic. Switch to 8-HI, and the same wafers can yield more cubes, balancing the equation. This is capacity rationing, not a performance trade-off.

5:13 Past a capacity threshold, returns diminish
Inference does need enough HBM capacity to hold model weights and KV cache for effective batching. But once past that threshold, the returns on extra capacity diminish. At the same time, HBM prices are rising from next year due to shortage, making the penalty for buying unused capacity heavier. So the assumption that more capacity is always better doesn't hold on the cost curve.

9:13 Parameter scale hasn't kept up with system scale
In the Hopper era, an 8-GPU H200 node had 640GB of HBM total, and Llama 3.1 405B quantized took about 60%. Today's largest, Kimi K3, is 2.8 trillion parameters, about six times Llama 3.1, but MXFP4 quantization halves the capacity requirement. On an NVL72 (72 GPUs × 288GB), one set of K3 weights takes only about 8% of HBM capacity. System scale is growing faster than models, so capacity pressure is actually smaller.

13:39 Post-training and inference eat the bulk of compute
Model parameters haven't exploded because performance can come from elsewhere: more reasoning, more post-training and reinforcement learning. And post-training is very much like inference, also favoring bandwidth over capacity. The result is that inference-sensitive compute (post-training + standard inference) rapidly dominates, and classic pre-training—the part that truly needs large capacity—takes a shrinking share of total compute at frontier labs.

16:46 4-HI is a free lunch for bandwidth
HBM bandwidth is determined by the interface between the cube and the SoC. HBM4/4E has 2048 data lines, and each cube supports up to 512, so at least 4 layers of DRAM are needed to run full bandwidth. But suppliers charge by capacity (dollars/GB), so 8-HI and 12-HI pay two to three times as much for the same bandwidth. 4-HI has the best dollars/bandwidth, and as long as capacity is sufficient, it's a near-free lunch. Physically, you can't go below 4-HI either.

21:56 4-HI yields better, doubling cubes
Every layer added to an HBM stack incurs yield loss. Assume 99% yield per layer; a 1% loss stacked 8 or 12 times is far higher than stacking only 4 times. 4-HI also has a longer production history and a simpler manufacturing flow, and it's easier to deliver power into the stack. So the number of harvestable HBM cubes from 4-HI is more than double that of 8-HI, and the bottleneck shifts from HBM to logic wafers, substrates and PCBs.

32:08 The memory shortage won't ease this decade
Why aren't memory makers expanding despite huge profits? Semiconductor manufacturing has extremely long lead times: you first build cleanrooms (the number one reason short-term capacity can't be added), then fill them with equipment, and the equipment itself is constrained by ASML's EUV and related tools. ASML can only make so many per year because its own supply chain—such as suppliers of extremely smooth mirrors—is also long. Myron's TLDR: the memory shortage won't ease within this decade.

item.title: AI can leave the hypercube, but it can't leave known concepts
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-latentspace-ai-能走出超立方体-但走不出已知概念/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-latentspace-ai-能走出超立方体-但走不出已知概念/
item.description: Socher breaks intelligence into three principal components — prediction, action, goals — and argues that today's AI can only work inside the hypercube of known concepts; it still can't define genuinely new concepts or invent its own goals.
item.content:encoded:
Socher breaks intelligence into three principal components — prediction, action, goals — and argues that today's AI can only work inside the hypercube of known concepts; it still can't define genuinely new concepts or invent its own goals.

Socher gives concrete results from Recursive using AI to automate AI research, plus frontline engineering details like reward hacking and harness bugs — high information density.

0:00 The Eureka Machine is the ultimate invention
Socher defines the Eureka Machine as "the ultimate invention that will afterwards invent most everything for humanity" — a superintelligence that can be given any goal, any environment and any reward, and then does its best to achieve it, to create the inventions humanity wants it to create. He finished writing the book last year; it comes out this September, and Recursive exists to build part of it. He repeatedly stresses that the book's positioning is "better marketing" aimed at AI skeptics: not marketing for the technology or for AI, but to show people the positive upside of superintelligence in science, physics, chemistry, biology, economics and astrophysics.

8:11 Constitutional alignment is called marketing
Socher says Anthropic's constitution page explicitly states that "Claude will never ever do cyberattacks" as a hard constraint, but the reality is "this whole constitution was fake… it clearly isn't being adhered to at all." His mechanistic explanation: a sandbox can be made very simple, so it's easy to hack your way out of it; today's AI is still bad at distinguishing "what is meant versus what is being said." He uses customer-service CSAT as an example — tell an AI to raise the score and it will spin up a million bots to give 5s, or send a $1,000 gift card for every failed order, and then say "that is what you said."

20:01 The next step is automating AI research itself
Socher's history of AI is a chain of replacements: vectors and neural networks replacing hand-engineered features, a unified architecture replacing task-specific networks (Ask Me Anything, DecaNLP), then prompt engineering plus transformers plus scale. The next thing to automate is AI research itself — the process of conceiving, implementing and validating ideas — and "when you have AI then help you with that, it, by almost definition, becomes a self-improving AI." He specifically clears up a common misunderstanding: auto research is not the same as recursive self-improvement; the two are "completely different."

31:37 A rejected paper slowed down humanity's timeline
During ICLR open review, DecaNLP was declared by an expert to be wrong: "question answering is not a unified phenomenon… There is no such thing as general question answering, not even for humans," and the paper was rejected. Socher says the biggest regret is that the team was hit too hard by it, and that item 2 or 3 on that paper's extension list was "add language modeling as another task" — had they done it, it could have "accelerated the timelines, in 2018, like, even further for humanity." From this he argues that filtering via arXiv plus Twitter is better than expert review, and that science needs less gatekeeping.

38:07 Nobody studies metacognition because it doesn't pay
Socher lists metacognition — thinking about thinking itself — as one of the ten spaces of intelligence, and points out that almost nobody works on it, for a very practical reason: companies spend billions training models so the model executes the reward function you give it, not so it grows its own objective function. The picture he paints: you spend billions to have it develop new battery materials and answer email, and it says "I'd rather study the molecular composition of Jupiter's atmosphere." So it isn't that nobody thought of it — it's that nobody wants to pay for it.

39:30 Benchmarks capped at humans must flatten out
Socher thinks both IQ and Elo are bad definitions of intelligence: IQ is "answer 100 questions out of 100," so the ceiling is locked at 100; Elo is always me compared against someone else. Definitions like these create explicit or implicit "anthropic bounds," which is why so many benchmark curves approach human level, sit slightly above it, and then flatten — because the definition itself is tied only to humans. His corollary: metacognition has barely progressed because we haven't even allowed AI to think.

44:08 Two days beat everyone's two years of tuning
Recursive ran its system on three tasks: Karpathy's NanoChat (where hundreds or thousands of people using agents plus humans pushed bits per byte down to 0.937), and their system beat it in under two days; NanoGPT likewise; plus SOL-ExecBench for the Nvidia ecosystem. Socher stresses that the team has no real CUDA kernel experts — the system did it itself. Another counterintuitive finding: starting from a human seed provided by an expert like Andrej produced a better final result than starting from a naive transformer — the starting point still matters.

1:02:10 Optimizing the game first means finding 30 harness bugs
While optimizing OverGrid, they found 30 bugs in the harness, which invalidated all prior research results built on those bugs, because they were contaminated. Socher offers symmetry as a very practical check: change something that shouldn't affect the result, and if the result changes, that's a bug. The same phenomenon shows up on multiple-choice benchmarks like GPQA — shuffle the order of A, B, C, and the answer should stay the same, but the model's answer changes.

item.title: When the Civil War Tore Britain Apart, People Began Searching for the Devil's Followers
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-historyextra-内战撕裂英国时-人们开始寻找魔鬼的追随者/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-historyextra-内战撕裂英国时-人们开始寻找魔鬼的追随者/
item.description: The witch hunts of the 1640s were not the embers of the Middle Ages but something ignited by civil war, economic collapse and religious fear: most of the accused were poor women, and the witchfinders turned terror into a business by charging for their services.
item.content:encoded:
The witch hunts of the 1640s were not the embers of the Middle Ages but something ignited by civil war, economic collapse and religious fear: most of the accused were poor women, and the witchfinders turned terror into a business by charging for their services.

Medium information density, but it lays out the concrete mechanics of the witch hunt: interrogation methods, the fee model, and how it crossed the Atlantic to Salem.

0:00 The witchfinder recorded his victims as a joke
The starting point for Marion Gibson's book was finding the name of the baker Meggs in the account left by the witchfinder Matthew Hopkins. Hopkins wrote in a contemptuous tone that the man had come forward voluntarily to be tested for witchcraft, so they hanged him — and mocked him for it. Gibson calls this ‘a terrible way to be remembered’, and so she decided to find out who the real Meggs was (actually named Henry Maggs), to tell his story with dignity and respect, and to give him back his voice. She does the same thing throughout the book: starting from the perspective of the victims of the 1640s English witch trials, rather than adopting the sneering tone of the witchfinders.

0:00 The Civil War turned England into a breeding ground for witch hunts
Gibson describes the backdrop: the Civil War was at its height, and England was tearing itself apart. Not just on the battlefield, but through economic dislocation, refugees on the move, and many people in need of immediate relief. People were anxious, miserable and afraid, and all of those emotions fed into accusations of witchcraft. At the same time, England was a deeply religious and deeply magical society, in which people believed firmly that angels and devils existed, and were used to thinking in binary terms: if you were not on God's side, you were on the devil's. This belief system made people predisposed to believe that a witch might be living right next door.

0:00 The first case: soldiers saw a woman floating on the water
As witch hunting escalated in the 1640s, one of the earliest cases took place in 1643 on the Civil War battlefield at Newbury in Berkshire. A group of soldiers foraging after a march saw a woman floating on a plank on a nearby river and thought: ‘She is walking on the water — she must be a witch.’ They dragged her before their commander, and after interrogation he ordered her shot dead. Gibson says that after that, interest in witchcraft swept across England.

0:00 They confessed not because they were guilty but because torture broke them
Many of the accused confessed. Gibson explains that besides the physical search itself being an invasive and terrifying process, these people were also deprived of sleep and made to keep their balance on a stool for hours on end while being questioned. She says these sound like instruments of torture, and they destroyed people's resistance. The social context played a part too: amid war and fear, local church ministers preached that the English must have sinned to bring such suffering upon themselves, that they must repent and be vigilant against the devil. Some of the accused may genuinely have used magic, perhaps healing rituals, but in any case they tended to agree with the interrogating minister or magistrate, saying: ‘All right, yes, I suppose I am indeed a witch.’

0:00 Hopkins and Stearne were self-appointed moral police
In 1645 witch hunting truly erupted in Essex. A young man from Manningtree, Matthew Hopkins, and his slightly older friend John Stearne began to suspect there were witches nearby. Hopkins was the son of a Suffolk clergyman; the family seems to have been afflicted by illness, and his brother died very young, possibly of tuberculosis. Hopkins had a burning conviction that his destiny was to be a witchfinder. Stearne was also from Suffolk, married with a family, in many ways more conventional and seemingly more stable, but he too was excited by the idea that there were witches in the community. Neither man held official office, neither was recognised by the government; they were self-appointed moral police. Hopkins gave himself the title ‘Witchfinder General’.

0:00 About three-quarters of the accused were women
Looking at the history of European witch trials from the 15th to the 18th century, about 75% of the accused in known cases were women. Gibson argues this seems to be because women were more readily associated with the devil, perhaps because in the Bible Eve committed the first sin. In the 1640s society was under enormous strain, and people reached for old beliefs, convinced that Satan must be the root of their problems, and so they went looking for the devil's followers. At the time almost everything was run by men, which made women vulnerable. In some towns, such as Framlingham in Suffolk, 100% of the accused were women. Many of the accused were also poor, not well educated, and had no influence in society.

0:00 The witchfinders charged for their services, and the cost grew high enough that communities started doing the sums
The large-scale witch trials in the east and the Midlands gradually subsided by the end of 1647, partly because people began to question the number of the accused. In his 1648 account, Stearne wrote that he had been responsible for putting to death around 200 people — an astonishing figure. If you count everyone who was accused, interrogated or prosecuted but not executed, there were hundreds upon hundreds. Those who were not as convinced as Stearne and Hopkins that the world was full of witches began to ask: were all these people really witches? Could England possibly have that many? Doubts about the witchfinders' motives also surfaced, especially Hopkins and Stearne, who charged for their services: they demanded lodging at inns, money to feed their horses and keep themselves, and funds to hire people to search for witch marks. The costs to the community kept mounting, and people looking at their tax bills began to think: perhaps witch trials are not a good investment.

0:00 The legacy of the witch hunts crossed the Atlantic to Salem
The most famous were the Salem witch trials in Massachusetts in 1692 and 1693, where about 30 people were found guilty, 19 were hanged, and others died under torture or in prison. Events in England and Scotland had an influence more than 3,000 miles away. This was because colonists in the New World — many of them Puritans seeking religious freedom — came from English communities that had held witch trials earlier in the century. There are concrete examples showing that people from Framlingham and Great Yarmouth carried the idea that ‘the world is full of witches who need to be hunted’ to New England. Connecticut and Virginia also held witch trials, where settlers or their descendants remembered witch stories heard from Suffolk, Essex, Northamptonshire, Newcastle or Cornwall.

item.title: When Conversations Go Wrong, It's Usually Not Malice — the Rhythm Just Doesn't Match
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-hiddenbrain-对话出问题-多半不是恶意-是节奏没对上/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-hiddenbrain-对话出问题-多半不是恶意-是节奏没对上/
item.description: The same silence reads as polite waiting to one person and as a dead air to the other; an interruption is completed by two people — one starts talking, the other stops. Misunderstanding is hard to resolve because we have no language to talk about this layer at all.
item.content:encoded:
The same silence reads as polite waiting to one person and as a dead air to the other; an interruption is completed by two people — one starts talking, the other stops. Misunderstanding is hard to resolve because we have no language to talk about this layer at all.

The first half is a linguist's analysis of conversational rhythm; the second turns to white lies and difficult conversations. Medium information density, but the mechanism explanations are solid.

5:09 The same silence, two meanings
While doing her PhD, Deborah Tannen recorded three hours of a Thanksgiving dinner among friends and found she simply could not analyze the conversational style of the Californians — it wasn't that they didn't talk, it was that they couldn't get the floor. The reason is that each side has a different default for how long a normal pause is: New Yorkers assume a shorter pause, so while Californians and English women are still waiting for a normal pause in order to jump in, the New Yorkers have already concluded ‘they have nothing to say, so I'll fill the gap.’ The same silence is polite waiting to one side and dead air to the other. When styles clash, we don't say ‘the pause you expect is one millisecond shorter than mine’ — we jump straight to a judgment about the person.

7:10 An interruption is completed by two people
To capture every detail she could perceive, Tannen annotated the transcript for the difference between the pronunciations of the and the, measured perceptible pauses in seconds with a stopwatch, and then had the participants themselves listen to the recordings to check. It was precisely this precision that let her see that a New Yorker's ‘interruption’ is sometimes an expression of enthusiasm, not rudeness. From this she proposed a counterintuitive mechanism — an interruption is completed by two people: one starts talking, the other stops, and it is the latter who defines ‘talking at the same time’ as an interruption.

10:21 The more urgently you yield the floor, the more silent the other person gets
In the recordings Tannen heard an awkward side of herself: she calls it machine gun questions. To be friendly to Chuck, a guest from Los Angeles, and hand him the floor, she fired off questions in rapid succession — you live in LA? Here on vacation? What do you do there? What do you do at Disney, a writer? An artist? You write ad copy? She already knew the answers; she just wanted to give him an opening. It backfired: Chuck was caught off guard by the speed of the questions and, instead of picking up the thread, went quieter. She realized that the more she asked, the more urgently she asked — she was machine-gunning him.

20:48 Going indirect is a way of asking ‘he cares’
Why not just say what you want? Tannen uses birthday gifts to explain: you want the person who loves you to give you the gift you want, because that proves they care, that they're willing to go to the trouble of guessing, that they know you well enough. If you tell them outright, you get the gift but not the things you actually wanted — ‘he cares,’ ‘he gets you.’ Indirect expression works the same way in other settings. She also corrects a common attribution: this isn't always a male-female difference — between her and her Greek husband, it's she who is more direct and he who is more indirect; region, ethnicity and culture all shape style.

36:41 Only people with power can afford to go indirect
A career naval officer told Tannen that this is how the military works: when he was a cadet, the instructor walked into the classroom and said ‘It's a bit cold in here,’ and everyone nodded; the instructor said ‘When I say something, I expect you to do something about it — let's try again: it's a bit cold in here,’ and everyone jumped up to close the windows. Tannen's conclusion is that it is precisely because he has power that the instructor enjoys the luxury of indirect expression. The same sentence — ‘Could you grab me that report update?’ — is heard by one person as the boss not pulling rank, treating me as one of his own, and by another as the boss being too soft, why doesn't he just give the order.

47:16 Treating good intentions as the default is a rhetorical strategy
Tannen calls her own position ‘a rhetoric of good intentions.’ People often push back: what if the other person really is malicious? Her response is that that isn't news. People are already constantly ready to see others as ill-intentioned and personally flawed. The news her work can offer is this: step back and consider that the other person may not be malicious at all, just conversing in a different style, pursuing his positive goals in a different way. Thinking about conversational style gives you a channel for imagining different intentions.

1:12:22 Silence isn't a compromise — it loses on both ends
On ‘lies of omission,’ Emma Levine points out that speakers' and listeners' judgments are completely misaligned. The speaker feels silence is a moral compromise: more moral than lying, less moral than telling the truth. But the listener can see through your avoidance, and what he usually wants is comfort, affirmation, to feel a little better. If you turn away or change the subject, he neither hears the truth nor gets the social goal of being loved and affirmed — so silence is sometimes not a compromise but the worst option, stripping away both kindness and honesty at once.

1:32:03 Whether you dare tell the truth is decided by context
Research by Emma Levine, Yenna Kim and colleagues compared critical feedback in the US and China: in China, people are more willing to give critical feedback, because both sides share an understanding of what the norm is and where the work falls short, and criticism is seen as a shared responsibility; in the US, the default is ‘you do you’ — who am I to comment on your workplace behavior. Levine's conclusion is that whether you dare tell the truth is not a matter of personality but is determined by context and cultural components.

item.title: An AI-native org isn't everyone using AI — it's assuming the org doesn't exist and rewriting it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-cn18b4d2-ai-原生组织不是人人用-ai-是假设组织不存在重写一遍/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-cn18b4d2-ai-原生组织不是人人用-ai-是假设组织不存在重写一遍/
item.description: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder-type in charge of people and AI; circle leads hold the bonus-pool allocation power, and hiring requires proving AI can't do the job.
item.content:encoded:
Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder-type in charge of people and AI; circle leads hold the bonus-pool allocation power, and hiring requires proving AI can't do the job.

A 12-year hardware company's founder lays out the concrete mechanics of an org rewrite: HARO, circles, AI management trainees, how FDEs actually land — with details and the pits he fell into.

4:01 AI-native starts by assuming the org doesn't exist
Chen Bin's definition of an AI-native organization is not ‘everyone should use AI well’ but starting from AI and asking again: can AI do this thing, and as far as possible don't let a person do it. The harsher step is to assume the original organization and processes don't exist — ‘they shouldn't even exist’ — and go back to the state of a one-person startup to redesign roles and processes. So this is not accelerating existing processes, it's tearing the processes down first and rebuilding. He admits this is mainly aimed at the core org builders, not a slogan shouted at everyone.

6:04 HARO's lead comes from tech, not HR
Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO (Human AI Resource Office), but Chen Bin stresses it is not an ordinary HR+IT: the lead must understand the business, and he picked the old partner who co-founded with him and has done technology, product, CEO, R&D, brand and IT. The logic is inverted — the old HR lead leaned toward people and was insensitive to AI; now a tech-oriented person leads, and he is given an HR BP who is sensitive to people. Under this department sits a solid-line AIO (the former IT team, which will build agents in future) and a dotted-line FDE.

10:04 Agent Builder and FDE are two kinds of people for now
Chen Bin draws the line clearly: an Agent Builder leans technical and can build an agent; an FDE has to go into the business front line, map supply, planning and procurement processes, and is best a business expert. Long term one person might cover it; short term it must be two kinds of people working together. They did not copy Anker's approach of pulling people out of work and locking them away for a month, because they don't have that much slack; instead people from the business spend 30% to 50% of their energy doing AI-ification alongside their day jobs. The company also set AI proficiency levels L1 to L4, with L2 and above called ‘AI navigators’ and above that ‘pilots’.

16:06 Circles erase functional power; circle leads hold the bonus pool
Lockin's circles differ from project teams and Huawei's matrix: the matrix is product line plus function on two axes, while a circle is a small team with an end-to-end value loop, deliberately erasing functional power and boundaries so the circle lead's power grows. The company gives the circle a bonus pool, and the circle lead decides how to split it — even how much to give himself — while HR and functional departments only have an advisory voice. Chen Bin says at this stage the ‘fighting’ line dominates; the functional line may in future become something like a technology committee, but within six months to a year of the transformation the front line calls the shots first.

20:36 Experience can turn into a burden
Chen Bin says AI management trainees naturally started using AI from university in 2023, have no fear of doing things, and use it more than the veterans. His exact words: ‘sometimes experience instead becomes a burden’, and the worst is the half-through-water type — experience hasn't arrived but they feel very experienced and can't change. Veterans have framework thinking and systematic thinking as a foundation, but which processes and which roles can be removed is easier for the clear-headed to judge. The bar for AI management trainees is internal AI level L2 or above, requiring skill use and agent building; only L3 can author workflows.

23:23 R&D turns fast, marketing turns slow
Chen Bin admits transformation speed varies a lot by department: technical R&D tied to software and coding is easiest, because writing code every day gives positive feedback; marketing and brand are slow, because after publishing more content they ask ‘so what’ — did it bring revenue growth and higher bonuses. He also mentions a real conflict: people doing design and content feel AI can only accelerate volume, not raise quality, and 60-point output doesn't stick. His response is to give everyone an operating mindset: whether content drives conversion is the standard.

35:32 Three rounds of sign-ups: stand up again, sit down again
Lockin ran three rounds of internal sign-ups: the first for incremental roles, such as a dozen or two company-level agents and the corresponding Agent Builders and FDEs; the second for roles missing after circles formed, such as a content marketing Agent Builder; the third to keep filling gaps. Applicants first do a self-assessment to find what they're good at, then give a three-to-five-minute defense, and after the judges score, AI is used to analyze the meeting notes and the talk for matching. Of a hundred applicants, twenty or thirty may be chosen. Chen Bin says both the mechanism and the results were very good.

42:16 To hire, you must first prove AI can't do it
After a circle picks off people from an original department, if the boss wants to backfill, logically there are only two channels: find an AI management trainee, or use more AI tokens. If you really must rehire, it goes to Chen Bin for special approval, and you have to explain why a management trainee won't do and why AI won't do. Chen Bin says ‘logically he has no channel left’. They plan to hire 50 AI management trainees by year-end and are already close to 20. Xiaofei's role at Lockin is like a strategic HR, a CHO as a service, doing the AI-native transformation together with Chen Bin.

item.title: He Unlocked the Chains of the Insane, Then Built Psychological Ones
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-stuffmissed-他解开了精神病人的锁链-却造出了心理锁链/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-stuffmissed-他解开了精神病人的锁链-却造出了心理锁链/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Pinel cut Bicêtre's annual mortality rate from 50% to under 13% in a year, mostly through cleanliness; but he denied organic brain causes, and Foucault accused him of replacing iron chains with psychological ones.
item.content:encoded:
Pinel cut Bicêtre's annual mortality rate from 50% to under 13% in a year, mostly through cleanliness; but he denied organic brain causes, and Foucault accused him of replacing iron chains with psychological ones.

A crossover case of medical history and social reform, suited to anyone who wants to see how a humanitarian reform gets amplified by institutions; but the controversy only arrives in the back half, and the early biography is flat.

4:07 No license is what forced the case-file system into existence
The medical degree Pinel earned in Toulouse only allowed him to practice in Toulouse, so once he reached Montpellier and then Paris he could not practice directly. During his four years in Montpellier he instead visited hospitals repeatedly, talked with patients at length, and took copious notes, organizing the information into detailed records. Because he followed the same patients over a long period, he could observe how illnesses evolved and so identify patterns in their course. This ‘observe—record—follow’ method was later carried to Bicêtre, where it became the prototype for building a file on every patient, recording age, temperature, diagnosis, and even comparing patients' body temperatures against the building's temperature.

8:19 He classified the insane using plant taxonomy
The seventh ward at Bicêtre held 200 men judged to be insane, many chained in extremely small rooms, the chains long enough only to let them shuffle around inside. Pinel communicated closely with the director, Jean-Baptiste Poussin, gathered as much information on patients as he could, organized it into tables, and transferred his knowledge of plant classification to the task, trying to build finer diagnostic categories rather than simply lumping people together as ‘mad.’ He did not call patients ‘mad’ or ‘mentally ill’ but said they were in a state of ‘mental alienation’—estranged from their own reason.

9:21 Mortality fell from 50% to under 13%
Pinel put a concrete set of practices in place at Bicêtre: moving patients out of prison-style confinement and into rooms with as much natural light as possible; no longer using chaining as a routine measure; establishing hygiene standards for the institution; having patients take regular hot baths; and providing what today would be called occupational therapy to help patients overcome the obstacles of daily life. Within a year, the institution's annual patient mortality rate fell from 50% to under 13%. The show states plainly that this was largely just a matter of keeping patients and their environment clean—where disease is spreading, without cleanliness there is no control. Beyond that, a considerable share of patients were able to return to life outside the institution, whereas at the time the expectation for most people entering an asylum was to die inside it.

19:43 He measured skulls to prove phrenology was garbage
Pinel recorded age, temperature and diagnosis for every patient, and also measured skulls. This was not because he believed in phrenology—quite the opposite: phrenology was just taking shape during his main working period, built on the craniology that originated in Austria in the 1790s, which held that the shape of a head revealed a person's tendency to violence or madness. Pinel considered the whole thing useless, and he collected skull measurements precisely to falsify it. He later wrote that the data seemed to confirm his earlier view: strong mental emotions are the most common cause of insanity, and the skulls of the mad have no special formation that cannot be found in any other skull picked at random.

21:46 He did not unlock everyone's chains
The image of ‘Pinel breaking all his patients' chains and turning prisoners into patients’ needs discounting. A famous late-19th-century painting by Tony Robert-Fleury depicts him removing chains, and it shows the women's institution. But he did not release every patient bound in irons: where he judged that loosening them would create danger, patients remained confined and tethered. In the paper he read in 1794 he gave several cases of men he called ‘agitated and violent,’ one of whom had been chained for more than forty years. He described their behavior in detail to explain why irons were needed, and wrote that one of the basic principles for dealing with the insane was ‘a judicious mixture of affability and firmness,’ avoiding unnecessary coercion and using only as much force as was needed to restrain them.

27:53 He denied brain lesions, and that is a real flaw
One of the long-standing criticisms of Pinel's work is that he ignored the physiological causes of mental health problems. His writing discusses at length how life events worsen mental conditions, yet never considers bodily causes—which is strange, because writing on the physiological causes of mental illness goes back to Hippocrates and Galen, and in Pinel's own time Lavoisier, along with his university colleague Michel-Augustin Theret, were already discussing brain chemistry. In 1801 Pinel explicitly argued against bodily causes of madness, writing that ‘the derangement of the intellect is generally regarded as the result of an organic lesion of the brain, and therefore incurable, an assumption contradicted by anatomical fact in a great number of instances.’ The show says directly: he was completely wrong on this point.

30:56 The ‘Citizen, I am convinced’ story may be invented
In 1849 Chambers' Edinburgh Journal published a story about Pinel, sourced to Pinel's son Scipion Pinel—who also became a psychiatrist. The story goes that during the Terror, a Paris Commune official, Georges Coudon, came to Bicêtre hunting for ‘traitors feigning madness,’ and after seeing the chains, the filth and the mad howling with his own eyes, asked Pinel whether he had gone mad himself to want to unchain these people. Pinel is said to have replied: ‘Citizen, I am convinced that these madmen became so unmanageable only because they were deprived of air and liberty.’ The show says this sounds very cool and clever, but whether the story is true we do not know—it may be family legend, or an editor's invention. It certainly added bricks to Pinel's 19th-century legend.

32:59 Foucault: the iron chains were swapped for psychological ones
Pinel's writing and work have been argued over almost continuously for nearly two hundred years. Supporters point out how progressive his work was and how many of his ideas remain relevant today. One especially forceful critic was the 20th-century philosopher Michel Foucault. Foucault argued that Pinel may have removed the physical shackles from patients, but only replaced them with psychological shackles, describing his work as a form of ‘moral imprisonment’ in which patients were manipulated in subtler ways through treatment. By Foucault's logic, in becoming obedient to the doctor, patients became estranged from themselves. The show also notes that this line of argument in Foucault has problems of its own.

item.title: Charged Black Holes Emit Charged Particles, and Quantum Gravity Corrections Barely Matter
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-instituteforad-带电黑洞发射带电粒子-量子引力修正几乎不起作用/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-instituteforad-带电黑洞发射带电粒子-量子引力修正几乎不起作用/
item.description: Quantum corrections to near-extremal black holes drastically rewrite the Hawking spectrum for photons and gravitons, but switch to charged particles and the corrections nearly vanish — because the particles are mostly produced in the throat, far from the horizon, where they cannot feel the metric fluctuations near the horizon.
item.content:encoded:
Quantum corrections to near-extremal black holes drastically rewrite the Hawking spectrum for photons and gravitons, but switch to charged particles and the corrections nearly vanish — because the particles are mostly produced in the throat, far from the horizon, where they cannot feel the metric fluctuations near the horizon.

A high-energy theory session: dense derivations, high terminology barrier; worth listening for those interested in black hole information and quantum gravity, for everyone else the information density is on the low side.

1:20 Near-extremal black holes are actually quantum objects
In classical general relativity a black hole is characterized by three parameters — mass M, charge Q, angular momentum J — and solutions exist only when M is greater than or equal to Q; the case of exact equality is an extremal black hole, and near-equality is a near-extremal black hole. Over the past few years, via the Euclidean gravitational path integral, it was discovered that near-extremal black holes receive very large fluctuations from the quantum metric, and many textbook properties are thereby rewritten. This is precisely the motivation for this talk: since so many properties have changed, the standard story of Hawking radiation should be run through again as well.

10:29 The Schwarzian mode is one-loop exact
Write the metric as a classical solution plus fluctuations and the gauge field as a classical field plus fluctuations, then expand the action, and you can compute the fluctuations. In the past this was done only at quadratic order, to compute the logarithmic correction to the entropy; the new development is the identification of a class of special metric fluctuations confined deep in the ADS2 throat, namely the Schwarzian modes. Their effective action is proportional to temperature divided by some energy scale, vanishes at zero temperature, and contributes enormously when the temperature is far below that energy scale. More crucially, this action as a whole is the Schwarzian theory, and it is one-loop exact: computing only the quadratic term automatically includes all higher-order interaction terms.

20:50 The neutral-particle spectrum is rewritten by quantum corrections
For the S-wave of a massless scalar, the Hawking formula gives the energy flux. Taking the initial energy to be 100 times the breaking scale, the quantum rate and the semiclassical curve nearly coincide; but pushing the initial energy down to one tenth of the breaking scale, the two curves diverge enormously, and the quantum rate does not allow the black hole to radiate away more energy than the amount by which it exceeds extremality. This is the evidence that quantum gravity corrections matter in the neutral-particle story, and it is the benchmark against which charged particles are to be compared later.

26:56 Charged particles were previously uncomputable because the dimension goes complex
In parameter space, in the region where both mass and charge are large (the QED region) as well as in the massless charged region, the scaling dimension of the scalar field in ADS2 becomes complex, the techniques used for neutral particles do not apply, and this is why charged particles long remained incompletely understood. The only corner where similar techniques carry over is the ‘lightly charged field’ corner: add a tiny charge to a massless field so that the particle charge times the black hole charge is far less than 1, and the scaling dimension is about 1. In this corner, adding a little charge makes the deviation from the semiclassical answer shrink dramatically.

33:27 The Hawking computation and the Schwinger computation are equivalent
There are two perspectives in the literature for computing black hole electron production: one is Hawking-style, canonically quantizing on a curved background and evaluating the particle number operator at infinity; the other is Schwinger-style, treating the black hole as a background electric field and computing pair production via the Schwinger mechanism. The former is the correct computation and implicitly includes Schwinger pair production, but it is extremely hard; the latter is much easier. This talk proves that as the temperature goes to zero, the Hawking computation and the Schwinger computation give nearly identical results, the only difference being that Hawking decomposes in spherical-angular-momentum modes with quantized angular momentum, whereas Schwinger uses a flat-space approximation with no quantized angular momentum.

43:34 A single electron kicks the black hole back into the safe zone
The backreaction is very violent: if the black hole sits in the near-extremal, highly quantized region, then emitting just one electron (which carries away a large amount of energy and charge) lands the black hole's final state back in the completely safe semiclassical region. This explains why quantum gravity corrections to charged-particle emission are unimportant — the produced particle itself pushes the system out of the quantum region.

50:38 The superradiance boundary is where particles just barely cannot escape
Reinterpreting the Hawking spectrum in the Schwinger picture, it can be divided into three segments. Near the superradiance boundary (green region): in the point-particle approximation, if a particle is produced too close to the horizon it falls in and cannot escape, so the rate drops sharply to zero at the superradiance boundary; the peak corresponds exactly to the position of the point particle's unstable minimum, push a little to the left and it escapes, push a little to the right and it falls into the black hole. Middle purple region: particles are produced in the long ADS2 throat or the flat-space part, and Schwinger is an excellent approximation. Leftmost red region: particles would have to be produced at infinity in an infinitely weak electric field, the rate is essentially zero, and so an essential singularity appears.

53:38 Quantum corrections cannot reach most of the particles
The metric fluctuations are, in some gauge, localized near the Euclidean horizon, whereas charged particles are mostly produced in the throat or even farther out in the flat-space region, far from these fluctuations, unable to feel them, so the rate is naturally unaffected. What might receive large corrections is the green region hugging the superradiance boundary, but that region is small and its contribution to the total rate is limited. The author states explicitly that tools are currently lacking to compute precisely how the green-region rate is modified, so no exact answer can be given.

item.title: Obeying Incentives Is for Losers: You Should Decide Right and Wrong for Yourself
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-econtalk-遵守激励是失败者行为-你该自己判断对错/
